partOf.title: The Greek Neolithic: A New Review
partOf.abstract: The Greek Neolithic, here divided into five phases, is the oldest in Europe. Geographically, it is the closest to the Near East and has thus long been seen as an impoverished derivative of the latter. However, recent research has tended to emphasize the autochthonous nature of Neolithic development in Europe, including Greece. The Greek Neolithic economy, which was based almost entirely on domesticates, and its densely packed, long-lived villages strongly recall the Near East, as do also the early emphasis on fine, decorated, nonculinary pottery and the wealth of figurines. On the other hand, the evolution of stylistic patterns is specifically Greek, although generally related to trends in the Balkans. Originality in the development of the Greek Neolithic is also seen in its latest phase, with apparent decreases, rather than increases, in site density, social differentiation, and, to some extent, long-distance trade. At the same time, however, the dichotomy became much sharper between the rich agricultural plains of northern Greece and the more pastoral(?) regions of the Peloponnese and Cycladic Islands; this presages similar contrasts during the Bronze Age.

source.title: Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea

p03tcss.editorialNote:
The project Beta maṣāḥǝft: Manuscripts of Ethiopia and Eritrea (Schriftkultur des christlichen Äthiopiens: eine multimediale Forschungsumgebung) is a long-term project funded within the framework of the Academies' Programme (coordinated by the Union of the German Academies of Sciences and Humanities) under survey of the Akademie der Wissenschaften in Hamburg. The funding will be provided for 25 years, from 2016–2040. The project is hosted by the Hiob Ludolf Centre for Ethiopian Studies at the University of Hamburg. It aims at creating a virtual research environment that shall manage complex data related to predominantly Christian manuscript tradition of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Highlands.

The periods list is based on the traditional subdivision of Ethiopian history as it appears in E. Cerulli, La letteratura etiopica (Florence: Sansoni, 1968).

A new chart of history. To Benjamin Franklin LL. D.F.R.S. this chart is in testimony of esteem & friendship, inscribed by his most obliged humble servt. Joseph Priestley.

p05hrsfwxqw.editorialNote:
The chart depicts years with a chronological line at the top, radiating from a center point of the birth of Christ. "BC" has been added to the entries where required as illustrated by the structure of the chart, but not actually written.
Spatial coverage has been determined by the labels on the chart running along the right side, separated across the chart with horizontal lines, and narrowed within each horizontal line by smaller areas.

Strangely, Priestley pays almost no attention to the well-documented history of southern China; although he mentions the Song Dynasty, he only provides an end-date -- the beginning of Chinese history in the timeline is just the edge of the horizontal bar and the legend "Chinese". We have used the start of that horizontal bar as an arbitrary start-date.
p05hrsfwxqw.label: Chinese
p05hrsfwxqw.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "China", p. 85: "This empire is certainly of very great antiquity; but, like other antient nations, has been aggrandized by fables. The first monarch is said to have been Fohi, whom the defenders of Chinese antiquities pretend to have been the fame with Noah; but omitting these pretended antiquities, the first foreign invasion of China was made by the Kitans in 946... [Oktay] attacked the Song in 1235, and made them tributary in 1260, but they were finally conquered by Kublay in 1279."

In 1396 he invaded the rest of India, and in 1399 he entered Delhi the capital of it, conquering the remains of Mahmud Gazni's empire"; p. 83: "when Sultan Babr was expelled from Buccharia by the Usbeks, he was obliged to fight his way into India, where he firmly established himself in 1530, and conquered the whole of it, except Decan, Guzerat, and Bengal. In 1621 Shah Abbas of Persia conquered Candahar. In 1687 Golkonda and Visapour were conquered by the Moguls."

p05hrsf4xrb.label: Spanish Chili
p05hrsf4xrb.editorialNote: Spanish colonial activity groups together Mexico, Peru, Chile, and "Terra Firma" in the timeline, but the dates for the Spanish period in each area can be extracted from the form of the timeline.

p05hrsfmvth.label: Dutch Brasil
p05hrsfmvth.editorialNote: Refers to the northern portion of Brazil colonized by the Dutch during this period.

p05hrsfjgcc.label: Spanish Terra Firma
p05hrsfjgcc.editorialNote:
The spatial coverage of the province of Tierra Firme also includes French Guiana/Guyane, but this overseas department of France does not appear in Wikidata as of June 2020. Spatial coverage derived from a map of 1732 at https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:TierraFirme.jpg#/media/File:TierraFirme.jpg.

The shape of the timeline suggests a date range rather than a single date for the establishment of Spanish control in this area.

p05hrsfg7ng.label: Secular monarchs of Japan
p05hrsfg7ng.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Japan", pp. 86-87: "Sin-onu, an ecclesiastic, is said to have founded the Japanese monarchy, about 660 B.C. but in 1188 Jerotimo put an end to the supreme ecclesiastic authority, and became the first secular monarch of Japan."
p05hrsfg7ng.editorialNote: Priestley distinguishes between the absolute rule of the Japanese Emperor and the period of the Shoguns. Although the Shogunate technically began in 1192, Priestley seems to begin this period with Minamoto no Yoritomo's ("Jerotimo") rise to power from 1185.

p05hrsf6mg3.label: Khalkas
p05hrsf6mg3.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, p. 84: "At what time the Khalkas became independent is not known, but they were conquered by the Chinese Tartars in 1696."
p05hrsf6mg3.editorialNote: Although the beginning of the rule of this northern Mongolia group falls around the same time as the end of Mongol rule of Tibet in the timeline, it is unclear why the division is placed here. The end of this group's timeline seems to coincide with the incorporation of Outer Mongolia into the Qing dynasty.

p05hrsfpgrh.label: Eluths
p05hrsfpgrh.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, p. 84: "The Eluths became a separate state about 1400, and continue independent to this day."
p05hrsfpgrh.editorialNote: "Eluths" appear in 18th and 19th century sources as a western Mongol ethnic sub-division and/or a synonym for Kalmyks, although they appear to be active further east than the area occupied by Kalmyks in the later Russian empire. Since the Eluths are still shown as independent in the timeline, and since the Kalmyks were absorbed by China on one side and the Russian empire on the other in 1771, the Kalmyks are probably the people to whom Priestley is referring.

p05hrsf9hgx.label: Ethiopians
p05hrsf9hgx.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Ethiopia and Abyssinia", p. 87: "This country was ravaged by Sesac, or Sesostris the Egyptian, in the reign of his father Ammon, about 1008 B.C., but upon his death, in 956, the Ethiopians recovered their independency, and in 947 they invaded Egypt... In 671 Ethiopia was conquered by Asserhaddon king of Assyria, but it revolted upon his death in 668."
p05hrsf9hgx.editorialNote: Although neither the text nor the timeline are clear about chronology between 946 (when "the Egyptians, with the assistance of the Jews and Phoenicians, made Osarsiphus king, expelling the Ethiopians from Lower Egypt" (probably the small block at the beginning of the first "Ethiopian" section for Egypt in the timeline) and 671, the timeline suggests more precise divisions than the text. The timeline has two different "Ethiopian" divisions, both of which seem to distinguish between Egypt proper and "Ethiopia"; for the middle "Ethiopian" division, which begins between 780 BC (for "Ethiopia") and 750 BC (for Egypt), it is very likely that Priestley is referring to the 25th (Kushite/Nubian) Dynasty and the Kushite conquest of Upper Egypt.

p05hrsfcxgh.label: Assyrians
p05hrsfcxgh.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, pp. 87 and 89: for both Ethiopia and Abyssinia, the text notes that "In 671" they were conquered/subdued "by Asserhaddon king of Assyria, but they revolted upon his death in 668."

p05hrsff94b.label: Solomonic race
p05hrsff94b.editorialNote: This row is somewhat cryptic; it falls on the same line as the "Ethiopian" components that seem to have referred to the Nubian kingdom in previous periods, but its two temporal moments are "the end of the Solomonic race" in ca. 960 and "restored Abyssinians" in ca. 1300. These two dates strongly suggest that here Priestley is referring to the Axumite kingdom and its uncertain predecessors for the first part of this row (960 is the date at which the Axumite dynasty is supposed to have been overthrown), and to the Solomonic Dynasty of Ethiopia in the second part (the intervening dynasty was overthrown in 1270).

p05hrsf2pr3.label: restored Abyssinians
p05hrsf2pr3.editorialNote: This row is somewhat cryptic; it falls on the same line as the "Ethiopian" components that seem to have referred to the Nubian kingdom in previous periods, but its two temporal moments are "the end of the Solomonic race" in ca. 960 and "restored Abyssinians" in ca. 1300. These two dates strongly suggest that here Priestley is referring to the Axumite kingdom and its uncertain predecessors for the first part of this row (960 is the date at which the Axumite dynasty is supposed to have been overthrown), and to the Solomonic Dynasty of Ethiopia in the second part (the intervening dynasty was overthrown in 1270).

p05hrsf2xdw.label: Shepherd Kings
p05hrsf2xdw.editorialNote: It is unclear who Priestley is referring to by this designation; the dates are too late to refer to the Second Intermediate Period invaders now referred to as the Hyksos (Josephus' "Shepherd Kings"). The end date coincides with the death of Ramesses XI and the beginning of the the Third Intermediate Period. That the spatial reference is to lower Egypt/the Delta is inferred from the arrangement of this bar in the timeline.

p05hrsfbrjk.label: Egyptians
p05hrsfbrjk.editorialNote: Although this range overlaps with the "Shepherd Kings" and includes a period in which Egypt seems to control the "Ethiopians" between 1010 and 955 BC, Priestley's references are not clear enough to parse into multiple periods in different places, so the "Egyptian" segment here encompasses the entire chronological range but excludes Sudan and Ethiopia. Priestley is probably differentiating between Lower Egypt and the Delta (where he places the Shepherd Kings), Upper Egypt (always ruled by Egyptians), and the northern parts of Nubia, where Egypt made incursions at the end of the New Kingdom.

p05hrsfmgd4.label: Eastern Empire
p05hrsfmgd4.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Egypt", pp. 89-90: "In 30 B.C. it was reduced to a Roman province, and continued a part of the Roman empire, till it was conquered by the Saracens in 640."
p05hrsfmgd4.editorialNote: This period covers the continuous control of the Eastern Roman Empire in Egypt.

p05hrsf67dm.label: Eastern Empire
p05hrsf67dm.editorialNote: This period covers the renewed rule by the Eastern Roman Empire over Africa (except for Egypt) between the Vandals and the Islamic conquest.

p05hrsfkgp8.label: Mungls
p05hrsfkgp8.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, p. 84: "The Eluths became a separate state about 1400, and continue independent to this day."
p05hrsfkgp8.editorialNote: The spatial coverage of "Eluths" seems to be Western Mongolia and west to the west bank of the Volga, or the general range of the Kalmyks. The start date assumes that they were subjected to Genghis Khan in 1206, with the rest of this area, as noted in "A description of a new chart of History", p. 84.

p05hrsftqts.label: United-States
p05hrsftqts.spatialCoverageDescription: Nova Scotia, New England & New York, Pensilvania Maryland and Virginia, Carolina and Georgia
p05hrsftqts.editorialNote: The addition of "United-States" to a chart that otherwise seems to be the version published in 1769 can be explained as a later addition; we have not verified that this appears in the charts published in 1792, but those also had different credits for the writer and draftsperson. The inclusion of Nova Scotia in the United States is presumably an error.

p05hrsf2v3q.label: Gasnevides
p05hrsf2v3q.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th. ed, 1786, , s.v. "Indostan", pp. 82-83: "In 1001 Mahmud Gazni made considerable conquests in [Indostan]... in 1383 Timur Bek conquered Candahar. In 1396 he invaded the rest of India, and in 1399 he entered Delhi the capital of it, conquering the remains of Mahmud Gazni's empire."

p05hrsf8tjn.label: Patans
p05hrsf8tjn.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Indostan", p. 83: "In 1587 Golkonda and Visapour were conquered by the Moguls. The latter of these states was founded by Adel Shah, of the Patan race, in 1530."

p05hrsfbct4.label: Kitans
p05hrsfbct4.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, p. 85: "... the first foreign invasion of China was made by the Kitans in 946. In 949 some cities in the northern parts were relinquished to them, and in 950 they made further conquests. In 1117 the Kin Tartars, at the invitation of princes of the Song dynasty, who reigned in the southern parts of China, invaded and destroyed the empire of the Kitans, but at the same time made the Song themselves tributary."

p05hrsf5s3v.label: Japanese Corea
p05hrsf5s3v.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Korea", p. 86: "In 112 B.C. Ki-tze is said to have been the first king of this country, but in 201 after Christ, it was conquered by the Japanese, and it is uncertain when it recovered its independency. In 1224 it became tributary to Jenghis Khan, and in 1664 was conquered by Shunchi, the first prince of the second Tartar dynasty."
p05hrsf5s3v.editorialNote: While the text is entirely uncertain about the length of early Japanese rule of Korea, the timeline places the re-establishment of "Corea" with a dotted line at around 650.

p05hrsfhpgk.label: Japanese monarchy
p05hrsfhpgk.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "Japan", pp. 86-87: "Sin-onu, an ecclesiastic, is said to have founded the Japanese monarchy, about 660 B.C. but in 1188 Jerotimo put an end to the supreme ecclesiastic authority, and became the first secular monarch of Japan."
p05hrsfhpgk.editorialNote: The timeline marks the start date it with a dot for an event ("Japanese Monarchy said to be Founded") rather than a line for a political change.

p05hrsfsvkj.label: Chinese
p05hrsfsvkj.note: From "A description of a new chart of History", 6th ed., 1786, s.v. "China", p. 85: "In 1356 Chu, a Chinese, recovered Nanking from the Tartars, and in 1368 he put an end to the authority of the Mungls, whose dynasty is called Iwen by the Chinese. In 1643 the Manchew Tartars invaded China, and completed the conquest in 1645."
p05hrsfsvkj.editorialNote: The extent of this section of the timeline suggests that Priestley is referring to the entire extent of China -- north, south, and Leautong.

p05hrsf.editorialNote:
As of June 2020, this authority contains only the complete periodization of the first four major rows of spatial coverage in Priestley's chart ("America", "Africa", "China", and "India"), as they appear at https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1e/A_New_Chart_of_History_color.jpg. Note that this digital image, derived from a print work in the library of the University of Oregon and used in an interactive project by Daniel Rosenberg at https://pages.uoregon.edu/infographics/timeline/pages/index.html, appears to be from the original 1769 publication, but someone has added the United States after the English colonies at 1776 (after the publication date). We have included this addition, which seems to be specific to this particular chart. 

The authority may be updated with additional period definitions from the rest of the chart at a later date (contributions by volunteers are welcome).

Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA)
source.abstract: The Digital Index of North American Archaeology (DINAA) project is developing the first online, integrated, and comprehensive database of evidence for North America’s human settlement. DINAA provides a free and open framework to examine multidisciplinary questions of human-environmental relationships, at multiple geospatial and temporal scales. The project launched in 2011 as a publicly accessible compilation of existing archaeological site file, collection, and report data from multiple regional, state, and local repositories, linked with environmental and paleoenvironmental datasets. DINAA embraces current best practices in scientific data-management. These include open standards and open licensing, transparent version control (of both data and source code), Linked Data, and iterative development. In consultation and cooperation with government, academic, and tribal stakeholders, our team is now completing the first ‘proof of concept’ phase of the project. We have already linked site file information from much of the eastern United States, demonstrating the capability to develop a truly continental database.

p08x7cz8f39.note:
p.92: "Schwieriger und unsicherer ist es, die Zeit festzustellen,in welche etwa der Anfang dieser Kunslweise zu setzen ist, und ich sehe keinen festen Punkt, woran man eine sichere Schlufsfolge knüpfen könnte. Doch ist die Betrachtung nicht ohne Gewicht, dafs, bei allerdings vorhandenen Unterschieden in der Behandlung, doch im Ganzen sämmlliche Gefäfse dieses Styls ein ziemlich gleichartiges Gepräge tragen, und defshalb die einzelnen der Zeit nach wohl schwerlich zu weit auseinandcrliegen mögen. Bedenkt man aufserdem die allgemeinen Zeitverhältnisse, welche auch auf diesen Kunslzweig
ihren Einflufs ausüben mufsten, so wird die Annahme, welche auch Gerhard und Bunsen schon aussprachen, nicht ganz unbegründet erscheinen, dafs der Anfang eines eifrigen Betriebs desselben etwa in die Zeit der persischen Kriege zu setzen sei. Hiernach würden die Gefäfse dieses Styls im Ganzen und Grofsen etwa als zwischen Ol. 70 und 80. gefertigt angesehen werden könne"

p.92-3, n. 1: "Gerhard (s. Rapp. volc. p.53. Not. 4SI und 9''l9. *)) bezieht ein kleineres panathenäisches Preisgefäfs, auf dessen Rückseite ein Kitharöde dargestellt ist (s. Beil. antike Bildw. No. 649.), auf die von Perikles bei den Panathenäen eingeführten musischen Kampfe, so wie Bröndsted (l. c.) dem Emblem einer Sirene mit Doppelflöten,
welches auf dem Schilde der Athena mehrerer panathenäischen Preisgefäfse erscheint, dieselbe Beziehung unterlegt. Sind beide Vermuthungen auch wirklich richtig (die erstere namentlich hat gewifs viel Empfehlendes) und fallt auch jene Einfühlung noch später, als Ol.80., wohin sie Gerhard setzt (s. Plut. Pericl. c. 13.), so wird dadurch die obige Bestimmung keinesweges umgestofsen, namentlich da die stumpfen Mahlereien jenes Gefäfses anzudeuten scheinen, dafs, als sie gemacht wurden, diese Kunstweise nicht eben mehr gewöhnlich
war (s. oben S. 85.)."

p0dfxxpcnkv.note: Modified from Shea (2013*: 7, table 1.1), whose focus is on the Levant. *Stone Tools in the Paleolithic and Neolithic Near East. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge. These start & end dates are calibrated. A large regional chronological variability is observed here, as with the Epipaleolithic. Typically, the Neolithic on the islands is later than on the mainland, having derived from that region. However, an early Neolithic contemporary with that of the mainland has been recently documented in Cyprus; thus, the wide chronological framework is used here, which includes both Pre-Pottery and Pottery phases.

This end date is calibrated. The time range for the Epipaleolithic varies considerably, based on regions. For the mainland, the range is generally that given in this table; this is also when calibrated dates typically are used. However, for most Mediterranean islands, the Epipaleolithic often starts much later and continues into what is generally considered Neolithic on the mainland.

partOf.title: Exploration and exploitation in the macrohistory of the pre-Hispanic Pueblo Southwest

p0m9pcg.editorialNote: These are revised Pecos period definitions (including subperiods) derived explicitly from a large database of tree-ring cutting dates from across the Ancestral Pueblo Southwest. Basketmaker III is truncated to start at AD 500; Pueblo IV is truncated to end at AD 1400; all periods are rounded to the nearest 5th year. We wanted to identify the points in time when the rate of change in the cutting-date frequency was transitioning from slowing down to accelerating, to break up Fig. 2B into five Pecos periods (and their subperiods) based on the four primary “humps” in the cutting-date frequency distribution. To do so, we calculated the modal inflection points (the points at which a continuous vector switches from being concave to being convex, or vice versa) in a series of kernel density estimates of the number of cells with cutting dates through time (Fig. 2B), each using a Gaussian kernel (that is, a normal distribution). Because the smoothness of kernel density distributions is determined by the kernel bandwidth (here, the SD of the Gaussian kernel), we estimated inflection points for density distributions with kernel bandwidths ranging from 0.01 to 50 years, in 0.01-year increments (5000 kernel density estimates). For each density distribution, we calculated a series of inflection points as the years where the second derivative of the kernel density estimate function was zero. Kernel distributions with very small bandwidths will have many inflection points, whereas those with large bandwidths (that is, very smooth distributions) will only have a few. The inflection points of each of the kernel density distributions were combined to calculate the 10 most common inflection years. Inflection years were rounded to the nearest fifth year. One break in the P IV period (at A.D. 1365) was discarded because P IV was determined to not fit the demographic and organizational pattern of the earlier periods. All source code for defining these periods are available at http://advances.sciencemag.org/cgi/ content/full/2/4/e1501532/DC1.

SIA+ Chrono-Cultural Categories
source.abstract:
The document shows the chrono-cultural categories that are employed to classify archaeological entities within the Sistema de Información Arqueológica (Archaelogical Information System, SIA+) of Incipit CSIC.
Chrono-cultural categories are not exactly periods. They have strong chronological semantics but also possess cultural meaning. This is an arguable way to categorise archaeological entities, but nevertheless they have been used by Incipit CSIC on the SIA+ for over 18 years, and currently characterise over 200.000 entities from Galicia and neighbouring areas in NW Spain.

It is unclear whether author indicates the lifespan or the reign of Pyrrhus when indicating "the time of Pyrrhus" as the period in which the florid style gradually replaced the fine style. NOTES:

This table of major Chinese States and Dynasties provides a basic time frame, and includes both the overall periods, as well as specific sub-periods, or in most cases, specific states.

For example, the Northern and Southern Dynasties is listed (420 CE - 577 CE), along with the various states, such as Liu Song, Eastern Wei, and so on that existed during that period.    Note that the overall period is not itself a "state" and has no capital, nor any administration or political history.  It is merely a superset of many states.

By contrast there are Periods, with Sub-periods, such as the Song Dynasty, which was one continuous political entity, but is divided into two very distinct periods, the Northern Song and Southern Song, reflecting the incursion of the Mongols who seized the greater part of the northern area of the Song, and forced the capital to be relocated from Kaifeng to Hangzhou.

p0367jz.editorialNote:
Full reference: Ephraim Emerton, "The Periodization of History", Proceedings of the Massachusetts Historical Society (October 1918-July 1919), 52: 55-69. Available online at https://www.google.com/books/edition/Proceedings_of_the_Massachusetts_Histori/cfwKAAAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0. Spatial coverage in this work balances repeated references to "the world" by the author (taken as the source's assertion of coverage) with the apparently exclusive focus of the periods mentioned on Europe (as at p. 59, "If we confine our interest to that branch of the stream of history which chiefly interests us as heirs of the European tradition, we find ready to our hand the conventional division in to 'ancient', 'mediaeval', and 'modern'").

Emerton's paper actually proposes only five broad divisions of history, but he refers to the labels for the 16th and 18th centuries as common knowledge, so this work also attests to the currency of those period terms at the time of publication.

p0367jz87wj.note: "To save the meaning of "mediaeval" and at the same time to give greater clearness and validity to both "ancient" and "modern", it is worth while to carry on our process of division a stage further and to create for our use two additional periods, one preceding, one following that of the Middle Ages proper. If we think of this purely mediaeval section as beginning with Karl the Great about the year 800 and ending with Dante about 1300 these two new periods will then define themselves chronologically as covering respectively the years from about 400 to 800 and from about 1300 to 1600" (pp. 63-64); "At first thought these two added periods seem to be lacking in our first essential requirement, a distinctive character; but this difficulty grows less upon reflection. Superficially they seem to be characterized only by a greater degree of confusion than the others but, as we try to penetrate this apparent confusion, we see that it is better described as "transition"..." (p. 64); "And what has been said of the First European Transition is equally true of the second" (p. 65).

p0367jzcspk.editorialNote: "Middle Ages" used with capitals, passim; "mediæval" also frequent, with the same sense, but seems to be used slightly more generically in the section dealing with the proposed periodization

p0367jzzfpr.note: "To save the meaning of "mediaeval" and at the same time to give greater clearness and validity to both "ancient" and "modern", it is worth while to carry on our process of division a stage further and to create for our use two additional periods, one preceding, one following that of the Middle Ages proper. If we think of this purely mediaeval section as beginning with Karl the Great about the year 800 and ending with Dante about 1300 these two new periods will then define themselves chronologically as covering respectively the years from about 400 to 800 and from about 1300 to 1600" (pp. 63-64); "At first thought these two added periods seem to be lacking in our first essential requirement, a distinctive character; but this difficulty grows less upon reflection. Superficially they seem to be characterized only by a greater degree of confusion than the others but, as we try to penetrate this apparent confusion, we see that it is better described as "transition"..." (p. 64); "And what has been said of the First European Transition is equally true of the second" (p. 65); "Small wonder that this period was until lately neglected by the general student of history or that it has been claimed alternately by the historians of the Middle Ages and by those of modern Europe. It becomes interesting and illuminating when it is treated by itself as the Second European Transition... These two added periods, then, have a character of their own, the character of transition" (p. 65).
p0367jzzfpr.label: Second European Transition
p0367jzzfpr.editorialNote: The label assigned to the period and the reference to historians of modern Europe clearly indicates that this period refers to European history.

p0367jzb8hz.label: ancient
p0367jzb8hz.note:
"What we ordinarily call "ancient history" has a certain character of its own. It presents to our view a majestic succession of great empires, Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Greek and Roman; and these, with all their obvious differences, have certain common features. The theory of sovereignty is in each case the same. Each believes itself called upon in its own time to dominate as much of the earth's surface as it can reach with its arms or, in the case of Greece, with the even more penetrating weapon of its civilization. There is room in the world for only one sovereignty at a time, and the price it has to pay for its domination is the destruction of the world sovereignty that has preceded it" (p. 59); "Before the
year 400 the ideals of antiquity still dominate the world" (p. 64).
p0367jzb8hz.editorialNote: Start date is taken as the start date of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, which Emerton appears to treat as the earliest recognizable entity in "ancient history", presumably as a result of its relevance to Biblical tradition; end date taken directly from the statement on p. 64. Spatial coverage appears to be "the world" (as in "there is room in the world", but the spatial extent described on p. 60 is "the all-embracing sway of the Roman Imperium, turning the great Middle Sea into a Roman lake and reaching out northward and westward as far as the Roman legion and the Roman trader could penetrate."

p08m57h65g5.note: Western Europe: 450BC-43AD.  The term La Tène is used to describe the material culture of the latter half of the Iron Age across much of northern and western Europe, from 450BC to the Roman conquest. The name is derived from a site on Lake Neuchâtel, Switzerland, where the first 'La Tène' type objects were excavated in the late 19thC.  In addition to describing a broad chronological timeframe, the term La Tène is also used to refer to certain types of object characteristic of this period, for example a La Tène sword or brooch. La Tène can be subdivided into La Tène I, II and III, or La Tène A, B, C and D. Using these subdivisions well established typologies of La Tène objects have been created. For example, the attachment of the foot to the bow on La Tène brooches follows a pattern which is consistent over time and across much of Europe. For example, the foot of a La Tène I brooch is not attached to the bow. If a brooch of this type is discovered it is an important piece of dating evidence for other types of object.
p08m57h65g5.label: La Tène

p08m57hgs5w.note: 1040-1194 (AH 431-AH 590). Turkic dynasty ruling in Persia, Iraq and Syria that  reunited central 'Abbasid lands. The Seljuqs had originally their home in the steppes north of the Caspian and Aral Seas. They converted to Islam at the end of the 10th century. Under Toghril I Beg they seized Nishapur, the capital of the Ghaznavids in 1038 (AH 429). He entered Baghdad in 1055 (AH 447) and had his title of sultan confirmed by the caliph. The sultanate of the Great Seljuqs was based on a hierarchically organised state in the Perso-Islamic monarchic system, with the supreme sultan supported by a Perian and Arab beaurocracy and a multi-national army directed by Turkish slave commanders. Under Alp Arslan and his son Malik Shah the Great Seljuq empire reached its zenith and Isfahan was the capital. The Seljuqs founded various orthodox Sunni madrasas or religious colleges in Irag and the Persian lands and encouraged a synthesis of traditional theological and legal studies with the spirit of Sufism.
p08m57hgs5w.label: Seljuq dynasty

p08m57h54j8.note: Urban civilisation based in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, today in Pakistan and western India.  Developing out of earlier prehistoric cultures, it flourished over a very wide area between approximately 2,500 and 2,000 BC.  Script was known but is undeciphered today, not least as surviving inscriptions (mostly on seals) are no more than about a dozen characters.  Major settlements, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, were laid out on a grid pattern with drainage and were clearly organised by a central power.  The earliest fragments of woven cotton from the subcontinent come from these sites.  Trade with sites in the Persian Gulf, as well as with settlements on the Oxus, has been substantiated.
p08m57h54j8.label: Indus Civilisation

p08m57hg45z.note: This term is restricted to Iron Age numismatics, and applies to coins produced between 80 BC-AD 50. It refers to an area roughly equivalent to modern Hampshire and West Sussex, parts of Kent, East Sussex, Surrey, Berkshire and Wiltshire, in which similar styled coins are found. The various issuing authorities of this area seem to have relied on the same sources of technology and craftsmanship. Notable rulers in this area include Commios, Tincomarus, Eppillus, Verica and Epaticcus. The ethnic or tribal identities of these rulers and the anonymous issuers of earlier coins remain unclear, but they may have belonged to the Atrebates, Regni (or Regini) or Belgae (all attested districts of the later Roman province).  J Creighton, Coins and Power in Iron Age Britain, Cambridge (CUP) 2000.
p08m57hg45z.label: Southern British Iron Age

p08m57hmxmp.note: Classical World is a broad term referring to the civilisations of the ancient Mediterranean from around 1000 BC to 400 AD, centred on the idea of a continuous development of literature, ideas and material culture originating in Aegean Greece and its overseas settlements and later adapted and modified by the Roman state from the time of the late Republic and early Empire. The term was originally defined after the Renaissance by the literary and artistic inheritance of Greece in the fifth and fourth centuries BC and Rome between the first century BC and fourth century AD, but later took on a broader meaning including history, material culture, settlement and economy within much wider chronological and geographical parameters. The term also includes cultures in close proximity to or in contact with Greeks and Romans, such as Cyprus, the non-Greek peoples of Anatolia such as Lycians and Carians, and the Villanovan, Etruscan and Italic communities of Italy. Other cultures, such as Phoenicians and Carthaginians, local peoples of Spain and North Africa (including Dynastic Egypt), Phrygians, Thracians, Scythians, Celts and the Germanic tribes tend to be included under other Top Terms in the thesaurus (Prehistoric, Levantine and Middle Eastern periods and cultures, and Historic European Periods and cultures). Chronologically, the term sometimes is extended to the earlier periods of Greek history before 1000 BC, including the Bronze Age Minoan and Mycenaean civilisations based on the idea of cultural ancestry.
p08m57hmxmp.label: Classical World

The Ayyubids were continuing the policy of the Zangids in Syria and the earlier Great Seljuqs. After the death of the Ayyubid al-Kamil Nasir al-Din Muhammad in 1238 (AH 635) internal quarrels turned the Ayyubid empire into a confederation of principalities. The Mongol invasion put an end to Ayyubid rule.

p08m57hz9dg.note: This term is restricted to Iron Age numismatics, and applies to coins produced between 50 BC-AD 50. It refers to an area roughly equivalent to the modern East Anglia - Norfolk, Suffolk and parts of Cambridgeshire - in which similar styled coins are found. The various issuing authorities of this area seem to have relied on the same sources of technology and craftsmanship. The earliest coins were issued anonymously; later examples carry inscriptions that are assumed to be the names of local rulers. These include AESV, ALIIF SCAVO (or similar), ESVPRASTO, ECEN/ECE (if this is not a reference to the Iceni themselves) and ANTED. The ethnic or tribal identities of these issuers are unclear, but some may have belonged to the Iceni (who can perhaps be equated with the "Cenimagni" mentioned by Caesar - Caesar, De Bello Gallico, V.21).

p08m57hhcgp.note: 1250-1517 (AH 648-AH 923). The Mamluks (meaning 'one possessed, slave') arose from the Turkic troops of Ayyubids of Egypt and Damascus. Two lines of Mamluk sultans are distinguished: the Bahri Mamluks and the Burji Mamluks. The Bahris were ethnically Turkic from the southern Russian steppes with a mixture of other races including Kurds and also Mongols. The Burjis were Circassians from the Christian areas of the northern Caucasus. The Mamluks continued the strongly Sunni policy of the Ayyubids with the sultans, governors and amirs founding numerous mosques, madrasas and other religious and charitable institutions in Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo and elsewhere. They saw their role as defenders of Islam against the infidel Mongols, Frankish crusaders and heterodox Muslims in the mountains of western Syria. Egypt and Syria enjoyed considerable prosperity under the Mamluks until the 15th century.
p08m57hhcgp.label: Mamluk dynasty

p08m57hspv3.note: The term refers to a culture from c. 1stC to 3rdC AD. Knowledge of the so-called Indo-Parthians derives largely from coins and a few inscriptions. Some of the names and coin designs suggest links with the Parthians of Iran, but the precise relationship is not clear. In the first century AD the Indo-Parthians seem to have gained control of the region stretching from the Punjab, Sind and Gandhara (north-west Pakistan) to Seistan (south-east Iran). The principal ruler is Gondophares (c. AD 32–60). The title ‘Gondophares’ (Old Persian Vindapharna ‘Winner of Glory’) was adopted by his successors in addition to their given names on coins from Arachosia (Qandahar) and the Punjab. However, in Sind and Seistan they also issued coins in their own right as ‘king’ or ‘king of kings’. This suggests a complex situation of rulers and sub-rulers who owed varying degrees of allegiance to the Indo-Parthian king.

The Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204 (AH 600) gave the Seljuqs and oppurtunity to reestablish their power and extend their influence to the Mediterranean. With this and control over northern coastlands a flourishing transit trade developed between Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean across Anatolia to the Black Sea, the Crimea and the lands of the Mongol Golden Hoard. After circa 1225 commercial relations began with Italian trading cities.

p08m57h3sk2.note: Having previously been under the domination of their northerly neighbours, the Assyrians, native rule returned to Babylon in 626 BC, when Nabopolassar seized the throne. He was part of the coalition that would later destroy the Assyrian empire, and set the stage for the rise of the Babylonian empire. Perhaps the most famous king of the dynasty is his son Nebuchadnezzar, who in 598 BC captured Jerusalem and deported some of the population -- an event immortalised in the Bible. After a long and illustrious reign Nebuchadnezzar II died in 562 BC, to be followed by a series of kings with very short reigns. The empire fell in 539 BC when king Cyrus II of Persia overthrew Nabonidus, the last native ruler of Babylon.

p08m57hq7bs.note: Term used in Africa, Middle East and parts of Europe for assemblages of the early recent or Holocene period, after the end of the last Ice Age and before the beginning of farming, approximately 12,000-6,000BC.  These assemblages were used by hunter-gatherers and show few changes in content or technology from the preceding Upper Palaeolithic period except in the greater numbers of backed blades, crescents and microliths. This similarity gives rise to the term epi (like)-palaeolithic.  In northern Europe, environmental change was much greater at the end of the Ice Age, human adaptations changed in response and, consequently, the stone artefact assemblages are much different from those of the Upper Palaeolithic and are distinguished as Mesolithic. Despite this distinction the terms Epi-palaeolithic and Mesolithic are occasionally used as if synonymous.
p08m57hq7bs.label: Epi-palaeolithic

These coins were issued by the Arabs and Muslim authorities who governed the Sasanian provinces after the overthrow of the Sasanian empire. This coin type persisted in the eastern provinces of the caliphate for almost 200 years.  The Yazdgird Era, commonly abbreviated as YE, is the first era inscribed on Tabaristan coins and on some Arab-Sasanian coins. YE1 (ie. year 1 of the Yazdgird Era) corresponds to AD 632/633, the first regnal year of the last Sasanian ruler Yazdgird III (632/3-651).

A series of victories over the Persians culminated in the final battle at Gaugamela in 331 BC. Already ruler over Anatolia and Egypt, he now became ruler of Babylon and went on to extend control as far east as India. Following Alexander’s death in 323 BC, nominal kingship passed to his brother Philip III, with Perdiccas -- commander of the Companion cavalry -- as regent. In 320 BC Perdiccas was assassinated and rule over Babylon was allotted to Seleucus. He was forced out by Antigonus in 316 BC, only to return triumphantly in 312 BC.

p08m57hwwtz.note: 749-1258 (AH 132-AH 923). Dynasty ruling the Muslim world as caliphs with Iraq at it's centre and Baghdad it's capital. The Abbasids derived from the family of the Prophet Muhammad's uncle al-'Abbas and the Meccan clan of Hashim. The Abbasids were influenced by older Persian traditions of divine rulership. The Abbasid revolution, while in origin an Arab movement, began on Persian soil and took advantage of discontent in the Persian lands. The shifting of the capital from Damascus under the Umayyads to Baghdad in Iraq symbolised a new eastward orientation of the caliphate with increasingly evident Persian material and cultural practives of the next centuries. The Abbasid caliphs adopted honorific titles expressing divine support for their rule. The first three centuries of Abbasid rule saw the full flowering of medieval Islamic civilisation and influences coming in from Persia and the Hellenistic and Byzantine cultures. The Abbasid ruler best known in the West is Harun al-Rashid (786-809 AH 170-193), who is associated with the stories of 1001 Nights.
p08m57hwwtz.label: Abbasid dynasty

The second division of the Cypriot Bronze Age, marking an expansion in the range of pottery types (including White Painted wares which appeared at the end of the EC period), the spread of settlements all over the island (including fortified sites) and the first signs of significant overseas contacts in the form of numerous ceramic exports to surrounding regions. Many artefacts types, including metal goods, are similar to those from the EC and continue in use into the LC. The last phase of Middle Cypriot, MCIII, witnesses a major increase in the economic and cultural dynamism of the island, including the establishment of new coastal settlements.
p08m57h6tvb.label: Middle Cypriot

p08m57hkdk9.note: 1501-1722 (AH 907-AH 1135). The family traced its ancestry to Shaykh Safi al-Din who died in 1334 and is buried at the shrine in Adabil in north-western Iran. In 1501 (AH 905) Isma'il defeated the Aq Qoyunlu, seized Azarbaijan and took control of the whole of Persia. He declared Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion of Iran. The Safavids traced their lineage through the seventh Imam, Musa al-Kazim to ‘Ali, the Prophet Muhammad's son in law and his family. In 1514 (AH 920) Isma'il I and his army of Turkmen Qizilbash ('red heads' because of their red caps) suffered a humiliating defeat by the Ottoman Sultan Selim I at the battle of Chaldiran in north-western Iran. His son and successor Tahmasp I was either defending his western and eastern borders or controlling the Qizilbash. The most outstanding ruler of this dynasty was Shah ‘Abbas who drove the Ottomans out of the Azabarjian and established Persian control over the Caucasus and the Persian Gulf. Isfahan became the capital of Safavid Iran. Safavid rule collapsed with the invasion of the country  by the Afghan Ghilzays in 1722 (AH 1135).
p08m57hkdk9.label: Safavid dynasty

Timur acquired the title guregen/kureken, Mongolian for 'royal son-in-law' because of his marriage to a Chingizid princess. Timur was interested in settled lands of ancient Islamic or Indian culture and eventually built his capital at Samarkand (modern Uzbekistan). His rise to power began in Transoxiana. The later Timurids were mere local rulers in Khurasan and Transoxiana. The Timurid period was one of the most glorious periods in Medieval Islamic art in Transoxiana and Persia.

p08m57hmdw6.note: The term is traditionally used for the former territories of the Eastern Roman Empire, ie. Greece, Cyprus, eastern Balkans, parts of the Caucasus (Georgia, Armenia, etc.), Asia Minor, Levant, Egypt and parts of Italy, for the 6thC and 7thC AD. For the 4th and 5thC AD, the term Late Roman is preferred. The term ‘Byzantine’ can be used as an alternative .  The term ‘Late Antique’ is not used for the material culture of the former territories of the western Roman empire, ie. Italy, Gaul, Hispania, Britannia and Western North Africa (Mauritania, Tripolitania), for the 6th and 7thC AD. Instead, the term Early Medieval is preferred. Neither is 'Lare Antique' used for the broadly contemporary Sasanian Empire to the East (for which 'Sasanian' is preferred) or 'Early Islamic' and its Narrow Terms.  For non-Roman material (post AD 410) from Britain, the terms 'Sub-Roman' or 'Early Medieval' are used in preference to 'Late Antique'.  N.B. The Department of Greek and Roman Antiquities does not use the term 'Late Antique', see instead the terms 'Roman' and 'Late Roman'.
p08m57hmdw6.label: Late Antique

p08m57hs35q.note: At the height of its power, the Parthian state extended far beyond the modern political borders of Iran. It was ruled by the Arsacid dynasty and its first great ruler Mithradates I defeated his Seleucid overlords in a series of campaigns in the second century BC. Their earliest capital was at Mithradatkirt (modern Nysa) in Turkmenistan but they later established their capital at Ctesiphon in what is now southern Iraq and opposite the previous Seleucid capital of Seleucia on the Tigris. Parthia fought a number of wars with the Romans and at one period held much of Syria. The end of the period is marked by the defeat of the Parthian king Artabanus IV  in AD 224 by an Iranian noble called Ardashir who went on to establish the Sasanian empire.

p08m57hgrmh.note: 1650 BC-1050 BC.  The third major division of the Cypriot Bronze Age is marked by the appearance of new pottery types, such as White Slip, Base Ring and Monochrome in the North West of the island, which gradually replace older fabrics which continue in use from the Middle Bronze Age. Other important fabrics included Bichrome Wheelmade, Red Lustrous Wheelmade and various Plain and Painted Wheelmade wares; the latter are heavily influenced by imports from the Mycenaean world in particular (but also the Levant) which gradually displace the older hand-made wares by the 12th century.  The period is characterised by a thriving copper extraction industry, intense commercial interchange with surrounding regions – with imports visible from all around the Eastern Mediterranean - , and the emergence of more complex forms of social organisation, which can be called towns by LCIIC and LCIIIA. Literacy is attested in the form of documents written in a script called Cypro-Minoan, which has some links with Bronze Age Crete.  The last phase of the LC period, LCIII is a transitional period marked by major changes in the settlement pattern, burial practices, economy and material culture (including pottery types); the development of Proto-White Painted and Proto-Bichrome wares signal the beginning of the Iron Age in ceramic terms. The development of iron-making technology, in which Cypriot metallurgists played a leading role, develops apace at this time.
p08m57hgrmh.label: Late Cypriot

p08m57hz828.note: 661-750 (AH 41-AH132). First Islamic dynasty of caliphs, founded by Muawiya after the murder of  'Ali. The capital of the Umayyads was Damascus and from here the caliphs ruled over vast heterogenious territories. They adopted adminstrative practices of the Greeks and the Persians, the former rulers of the conquered lands. They introduced Sasanian techniques and manners which were strengthened under the 'Abbasids. During the reign of Walid I (705-715/AH 86-AH 96) they expanded militarily. All of North Africa west of Egypt was occupied and Muslim raiders crossed the Straits of Gibraltar into Spain. Beyond the Caucasus contact was made with the Turkish Khazars. In eastern Iran Khwarazm was invaded and Transonania gradually conquered. There was opposition from native Iranian rulers and their Turkish allies. Within the heartlands the caliphs faced constant opposition of Arab tribesman of Iraq. The Umayyads saw themselves not just as successors of the Prophet but as god's own deputies hense their title Khalifat Allah meaning 'god's caliph'. After 746 (AH 128) a revoltutionary movement began in Khurasan under 'Abu Muslim and the anti Umayyad forces gained military victory. This resulted in the succession of the 'Abbasids to the caliphate in 750 (AH 132).
p08m57hz828.label: Umayyad dynasty

p08m57hq6sd.note: 1050 BC-750 BC.  The Cypro-Geometric period, some three hundred years in duration, is the first division of the Cypriot Iron Age. Settlements founded during the transitional LCIII period become the urban centres of the city-kingdoms into which the island is divided in historic times. Economic and cultural contacts with the Levantine world with are re-established (or become archaeologically visible) after a short period of isolation; contacts with the Aegean become apparent again somewhat later in this horizon. Important ceramic types include White Painted and Bichrome wares, which are decorated with geometric motifs and often occur in inventive shapes; slightly later, the distinctive Black-on-Red wares are developed on Cyprus, partly as a result of contact with the Levantine world; fine metalworking in bronze abounds, particularly in burials. Inscriptions point to the existence of Greek and Phoenician speakers on the island living alongside the local Cypriot population.
p08m57hq6sd.label: Cypro-Geometric

p08m57h97b5.note: The term ‘Mycenaean' was originally used to describe Greek Bronze Age material of the period 1600BC-1060BC , following the discoveries made at the site of Mycenae by Heinrich Schliemann in the 19th century. However, ‘Mycenaean’ continues to be used to describe Late Bronze Age Greek material culture, particularly that relating to the palatial era, when sites such as Mycenae flourished.  The term 'Mycenaean' is used in preference to ‘Late Helladic’. Where a specific 'Late Helladic' sub-division term (such as 'Late Helladic I') can be defined, particularly in the case of pottery, the specific sub-division term should be used instead of 'Mycenaean'.

p08m57hph3k.note: This term refers to the Punic, western Mediterranean culture contemporary with the Iron Age and Roman Republican period. The culture exhibits elements of Greco-Roman culture but is essentially autonomous. It refers to Carthage and its settlements established in Sardinia, Spain and Western Sicily, and also to those settlements of North Africa around Carthage.  It is related to the Classical World but also to Levantine cultures as its origins are from the Phoenician settlements. This culture may thus be taken back as far as the foundation of Carthage in the 9th century (Roman sources date it to 814 BC) until its destruction by the Romans in 146 BC, but also may extend as far into the Early Modern period when it was refounded by the Romans until it was again destroyed circa AD 698.

p08m57h586b.note: Central Asian people of Sogdiana or Sogdia, centred on the fertile Zeravsham valley around Samarqand in Uzbekistan. It was a province of the Achaemenids (q.v.), invaded by Alexander the Great (q.v.), and was part of the Bactrian Greek kingdom until the Sogdians appear to have broken away c.200 BC and begun minting their own coins. The region was subsequently invaded by the Indo-Scythian (q.v.) and Yuezhi (q.v.) nomadic tribes in the 2nd century BC, but nevertheless remained a prosperous centre until the Mongol (q.v.) invasions in the early 13th century.  The Sogdians occupied a key position along the ancient Silk Road and, from the early 3rd century BC until the 10th century AD, played a major role in facilitating trade between China and Central Asia. They were the dominant merchants, their language became the lingua franca of the Silk Road, and they played an important role not only in trade but also in the spread of philosophies and religions, such as Manichaeism and Buddhism, to the east.
p08m57h586b.label: Sogdian

p08m57hf7b2.note: The term is used in relation to objects produced in ancient Judaea under the Hasmonean (c. 170BC-37BC) and Herodian (37BC-95AD) dynasties and during the two Jewish revolts (The Jewish War 66AD-68AD and The Bar Kochba Revolt 132AD-135AD).     From 301-201BC most of ancient Judaea was under Ptolemaic control; it was then under the Seleucids under Antiochus III Megas. By 40BC Judaea was almost entirely dominated by Rome, and the first king of the Herodian dynasty, Herod I, was appointed by a declaration of the Roman Senate. Coins minted under the Roman Prefects of Judaea ('the Procurators') have the period culture 'Roman Provincial', as do the later imperial coins minted in Judaean cities (e.g. Aelia Capitolina, the new Roman Jerusalem).    The term is not used for the collections in the Department of Greek and Roman. If the object dates to the period before Judaea became a Roman province (about 6AD) the term 'Hellenistic' is used, and if after Rome takes over then the term 'Roman' is used.

It may have been an early home of the Iranians. Khwarazm was under Samanid rule until it was added to the Ghaznavid empire under Mahmud in 1017 (AH 408). After the middle of the 11th century Khwarazm was under Seljuq rule. Since the time of Malik Shah the hereditary governors of Khwarazm received the title of Khwarazm Shah. After the conquest of Transoxiana by Genghis Khan in 1220 (AH 617) Khwarazm came first under the rule of Mongols and then Turkish Central Asian steppe peoples.

p08m57hdff8.note: This term is restricted to Iron Age numismatics, and applies to coins produced between 80 BC-AD 50. It refers to an area roughly equivalent to modern Essex and Hertfordshire, parts of Kent, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire, in which similar styled coinages are found. The various issuing authorities of this area seem to have relied on the same sources of technology and craftsmanship. Notable rulers in this area include Addedomaros, Dubnovellaunos, Tasciovanus, Dias, Rues and Cunobelin. The ethnic or tribal identities of these rulers and the anonymous issuers of earlier coins remain unclear, but some may have belonged to the Trinovantes or the Catuvellauni. Both are known from Roman sources describing the administrative structure of the later Roman province, but only the former definitely pre-dated the Roman invasion of AD 43. The term "Northern" was used by Hobbs in the BM catalogue (1996) but is often considered confusing.  J Creighton, Coins and Power in Iron Age Britain, Cambridge (CUP) 2000.  R Hobbs, British Iron Age Coins in the British Museum, London (BMP) 1996.
p08m57hdff8.label: Eastern British Iron Age

p08m57h2cv3.note: 750 BC-450 BC.  The economic and commercial trends of the Cypro-Geometric period (q.v) culminated in a flowering of cultural activity in the Cypro-Archaic period. The numerous city-kingdoms, whose wealth and power are visible in tombs and increasingly monumental architecture (including urban fortifications), appear as vassals in the historical records of the Assyrian Empire. Pictorial art on vases develops considerably, while three-dimensional representation, in the form of stone and terracotta statues deposited in large numbers in tombs, reaches impressive levels.

p08m57hn6p3.note: The Ice Age refers to the period between 2.6 million and 11,700 years ago during which climate varied through alternating warm and cold periods. Modern humans and many other mammal species evolved during this period.  During some cold stages (glaciations) temperatures dropped so much that continental and alpine ice sheets spread over vast areas. With water frozen to ice, sea levels also dropped providing humans and animals with opportunities to spread out across land bridges which were then submerged again during warm periods such as we live in today. Throughout the Ice Age, Britain formed part of mainland of Europe.  However, 'Ice Age' (as used in the British Museum records) is a term in popular use for the period of warm and cold phases between 126,000 and 11,000 years ago or, more narrowly, to the time after 40,000 years ago when fully modern humans arrived in Europe and North America.  The Pleistocene is a geological term used to refer to the same period of climatic changes as the Ice Age.  The Last Ice Age refers to the period of warm and cold phases between 126,000 and c.11, 000 years ago when fully modern people like us (Homo sapiens sapiens) spread around the earth.
p08m57hn6p3.label: Last Ice Age

p0zpgf95vjc.note: Following the common usage of historians of English literature, we will denote by the “Romantic period” the span between the year 1798, in which Wordsworth and Coleridge published their Lyrical Ballads, and 1832, when Sir Walter Scott died, when other major writers of the earlier century were either dead or no longer productive, and when the passage of the first Reform Bill, after more than three decades of political stagnation and repression, inaugurated the Victorian era of cautious readjustment of political power to conform to the economic and social realities of a new industrial age (Volume 2, page 1).

p0xkgmrm3m2.note: The works covered in this section of the anthology encompass a period of more than eight hundred years, from Caedmon’s Hymn at the end of the seventh century to Everyman at the beginning of the sixteenth. The date 1485, the year of the accession of Henry VII and the beginning of the Tudor dynasty, is an arbitrary but convenient one to mark the “end” of the Middle Ages in England. (p. 4)
p0xkgmrm3m2.label: The Middle Ages

p0xkgmr3brp.note: The Romantic period … is, tellingly, demarcated differently than any of the other eras that literary historians and anthologists include in their timelines. By convention, the boundaries delimiting those other epochs are either set by the regions of monarchs … or conceptualized as coinciding with the openings and closings of centuries … The date usually serving as the terminus of the Romantic age, 1832, represents a contrast to this pattern, strongly associated as it is with a signal political event, the first major reform of the British Parliament. A diverse range of dates have been identified as marking off the beginning of the Romantic period, but, almost always, each of these, too is associated with an event of tremendous political and social impact. (Volume 2, pages 3–4)
p0xkgmr3brp.label: The Romantic Period

p0rc4w79x98.note: "By the mid-seventh century (636) a new era commenced in the region of the Levant." (page 222)
p0rc4w79x98.label: Early Islamic Period

p0rc4w75rs7.note:
"The Nabataean presence in southern Jordan is indisputably attested in the accounts of Greek and Roman sources as early as 312 B.C." (page 9) 

"It is commonly agreed that by the first century B.C. at least, Nabateans had permanent settlements in Edom and throughout most of modern Jordan." (page 201) 

"The rest of the country will have remained under the Nabataean control, as part of their kingdom, until AD 106 when Trajan's troops subdued Petra and what was a Nabataean realm became the Roman province of Arabia." (page 208)

"Thus, the size and number of sites occupied during the Nabataean period in the study area is significant, specially when compared with previous settlements, and after the tangible gap in human settlement through the Persian and Hellenistic periods." (page 202)
p0rc4w75rs7.label: Nabatean Period
p0rc4w75rs7.editorialNote:
Start dates are derived from earliest attested presence of Nabateans and the latest agreed-upon possible date. End date is derived from the beginning of the Roman period.

Author mentions a Hellenistic period in connection to the Nabatean period but omits any distinct period of Greek/Hellenistic dominance in the chronology.

p0rc4w7hs7x.note:
"By the first half of the 16th century, the entire region of Greater Syria and Egypt came under the Ottoman rule. In 1516 Jordan was taken over following the defeat of Mamluk governor of Aleppo." (page 229)

"For the rest four [sic] centuries (until 1918), the country remained under the Ottoman political and administrative systems." (page 229)
p0rc4w7hs7x.label: Late Islamic Period

p0rc4w7dzj8.note:
"The end of this period in the East, particularly in the Levant, is
well established and commonly dated to the year AD 636 when the Muslim army
defeated a Byzantine force near the River Yarmuk in northwest Jordan." (page 215)
p0rc4w7dzj8.label: Byzantine period

p0rc4w7mg6z.label: Late Ottoman period
p0rc4w7mg6z.editorialNote: End date is derived from end of Ottoman period in 1918. (page 229)

p0rc4w7rwp5.label: Roman period: Provincia Arabia
p0rc4w7rwp5.editorialNote: The Roman period encompasses the period "Third century and the Tetrarch period." The 324 C.E. end date is the beginning of the Byzantine period.

source.title: Chronologies in old world archaeology

p0fk6s4.editorialNote: Periods are from Chapter Two, "The Periodization of Palestine from Neolithic through Early Bronze Times" by Lawrence E. Stager.

p0fk6s43365.note: "We have reluctantly retained the somewhat awkward and misleading nomenclature 'Pre-Pottery' and 'Pottery' Neolithic because of established usage." (page 24)
p0fk6s43365.label: PPNA

p0fk6s47r4c.note: "We have reluctantly retained the somewhat awkward and misleading nomenclature 'Pre-Pottery' and 'Pottery' Neolithic because of established usage." (page 24)
p0fk6s47r4c.label: PPNB
p0fk6s47r4c.editorialNote: Stager notes a highly debated gap between PPNB and the Pottery Neolithic periods. (page 24)

p0fk6s4vnzp.note: "We have reluctantly retained the somewhat awkward and misleading nomenclature 'Pre-Pottery' and 'Pottery' Neolithic because of established usage." (page 24)
p0fk6s4vnzp.label: Pottery Neolithic
p0fk6s4vnzp.editorialNote: Stager notes a highly debated gap between PPNB and the Pottery Neolithic periods. (page 24)

p0fk6s42ghf.note:
"What we have just summarized pertains to the latter part of the period, which came to an end probably ca. 3500 B.C., a CRD terminus based on radiocarbon dates (I-353, I-285, I-1341) from Nahal Mishmar and the initial phase of EB I, which was contemporary with the Early Gerzean, or Naqada II, of Egypt." (page 27)
"How much before ca. 4000 B.C. early Chalcolithic culture begins, its origin, and its relationship, if any, to the terminal Neolithic must remain unanswered questions." (page 27)
p0fk6s42ghf.label: Chalcolithic
p0fk6s42ghf.editorialNote: Alternate label "Phase IA" refers to the synopsis of "Periodization of International Trade" and corresponds with Amratian and Naqada I in Egypt. (page 40)

p0fk6s459bb.note: "this preurban period of EB I has been shrouded in confusing terminology, which reflects chronological uncertainty; this, in turn, has led to muddled periodization." (page 28)
p0fk6s459bb.label: Early Bronze I
p0fk6s459bb.editorialNote:
Stager notes that the Early Bronze Age can be subdivided further and according to north/south regional variation: Early EB I (North); Early EB I (South); and Middle and Late EB; and EB I Sinae (page 31-5). He uses relative chronologies and does not propose definite periodizations for these subdivisions. On pages 28-30, he outlines scholarly debate on Early Bronze Age chronology with geographical considerations. 

Alternate label "Phase IB" comes from "The Periodization of International Trade" and coincides with Gerzean-Dynasty 0 and Naqada II-III in Egypt. (page 40)

p0fk6s4bh6s.label: Early Bronze II
p0fk6s4bh6s.editorialNote: Alternate label "Phase II" comes from "The Periodization of International Trade" and coincides with Dynasties I-III in Egypt. (page 40)

p0fk6s4vqz7.label: Early Bronze III
p0fk6s4vqz7.editorialNote: Alternate label "Phase III" comes from "The Periodization of International Trade" and corresponds with Dynasties IV-VI in Egypt. (page 41)

p0fk6s475tv.label: EB IV/MB I

p0dkm29ss9r.editorialNote: Dates for this period are specific to the Sinai and are not made explicit in the general chronological table on page 1529, which groups the Natufian under Epipaleolithic.

p0dkm292h4j.label: Epipaleolithic
p0dkm292h4j.editorialNote: Corresponding cultural periods are Kebaran, Geometric Kebaran, and Natufian. Corresponding Ice Age in Europe periods are end of Würm III, Würm IV, and the beginning of the Post-glacial. The geological epoch is the end of the Upper Pleistocene (Quaternary) and the beginning of the Holocene. (derived from chronological chart on page 1529)

p0dkm292wdr.note: "Aretas I, the first known Nabatean ruler, is mentioned in 2 Maccabees 5:8. He is the Arabian prince from whom the deposed High Priest Jason requested asylum in 168 BCE. He may be the Aretas, king of the Arabs, mentioned in a Nabatean inscription from Elusa. The Nabatean royal dynasty at Petra may have been founded by Erotimus (Justin, Historiarum Philippicarum, XXXIX, 5, 5-6), probably the Greek name of Aretas II, who reigned at about the end of the second century BCE. Most of the Nabatean kings who reigned in Petra from that date until the abolishment of the Nabatean kingdom in 106 CE are known." (page 1181)
p0dkm292wdr.label: Nabatean kingdom

p0dkm294wgs.label: Early Arab Period
p0dkm294wgs.editorialNote: The Early Arab period encompasses the Umayyad period and the Abbasid period, which are not differentiated chronologically here. (page 1529)

p0dkm29z2m4.note: "The earliest of the Epipaleothic cultures is the Kebaran, to which the earliest mortars so far recovered are attributed. This culture, dated to between 20,000 and 15,000 years BP, is characterized by very small flint tools (microliths). Its later stage, characterized by an increasing number of geometrically shaped microliths (rectangles and triangles) is accordingly named the Geometric Kebaran (15,000-12,000 BCE)." (page 1345)
p0dkm29z2m4.label: Geometric Kebaran
p0dkm29z2m4.editorialNote: Dates here are site-specific and differ from the Sinai Geometric Kebaran (12,500 BCE - 10,900 BCE). The general chronological table on page 1529 groups the Geometric Kebaran under the Epipaleothic and does not provide distinctive dates.

p0dkm29q4nc.label: Upper Paleolithic
p0dkm29q4nc.editorialNote:
This period's cultures are subdivided into Phase I ("Emireh," "Boqer Tahtit") (45,000 BCE - 35,000 BCE); Phase II (Ahmarian tradition) and Phase III-V (Aurignacian tradition) (35,000-18,000 BCE).

 The corresponding Ice Age in Europe periods are Würm III and part of Würm IV. The corresponding geological epoch is the middle of the Upper Pleistocene (Quaternary). (page 1529 chronological tables)

p0dkm292q3s.label: Pre-Pottery Neolithic
p0dkm292q3s.editorialNote: Corresponding cultures are Phase A, Phase B, and Phase C. Corresponding Ice Age in Europe period is during post-glacial. Corresponding geological epoch is during Holocene.

p0dkm2929sm.label: Acheulean
p0dkm2929sm.editorialNote: Dates here are site-specific, do not necessarily apply to this period at other sites, and are not made explicit in the general chronological table on page 1529, where the Acheulean is encompassed by the Lower Paleolithic. The Sharon Plain Acheulean differs from the Sinai Upper Acheulean (500,000-150,000 years BP).

p0dkm295x6w.note: "The earliest of the Epipaleothic cultures is the Kebaran, to which the earliest mortars so far recovered are attributed. This culture, dated to between 20,000 and 15,000 years BP, is characterized by very small flint tools (microliths)." (page 1345)
p0dkm295x6w.label: Kebaran
p0dkm295x6w.editorialNote: In the general chronological table on page 1529, the Kebaran is grouped under the Epipaleolithic without its own distinctive dates.

p0dkm29rd3w.note: "Aretas I, the first known Nabatean ruler, is mentioned in 2 Maccabess 5:8. (page 1181)

p0dkm29rd3w.editorialNote: The early Nabatean coincides with the Hellenistic, so dates are derived from dating of the Hellenistic period in the chronological table on page 1529. This period does not refer to the Nabatean kingdom (first attested in 168 BCE and abolished by Romans in 106 CE), but rather Nabatean settlement and inhabitation.

p0dkm29j944.label: Chalcolithic
p0dkm29j944.editorialNote: Corresponding cultural periods are Early phase and Ghassulian phase (derived from chronological table on page 1529).

p0dkm297tfn.label: Late Arab period

p0dkm299jb5.label: Mousterian
p0dkm299jb5.editorialNote: Dates here are site-specific, do not necessarily apply to this period at other sites, and are not made explicit in the general chronological chart on page 1529, which groups Mousterian under Middle Paleolithic. p0dkm292f42.label: Early Roman period
p0dkm292f42.editorialNote: Encompasses the Herodian period, 37 BCE-70 CE (page 1529).

p0dkm29x4q9.label: Middle Paleolithic
p0dkm29x4q9.editorialNote: Corresponds to Micoquian "pre-Aurignacian", Yabrudian, Mousterian cultural periods; Riss-Würm, Würm I, Würm II periods in Ice Age in Europe; and the early Upper Pleistocene (Quaternary) geological epoch. (derived from chronological table on page 1529)

p0dkm29tdvv.note: "On the basis of carbon-14 dates obtained from organic material from these sites, this culture is dated to about 12,500 to 10,900 BCE." (page 1385)
p0dkm29tdvv.label: Geometric Kebaran
p0dkm29tdvv.editorialNote: The periodization of the Geometric Kebaran in the Sinai differs from the periodization in the Sharon Plain (15,000-12,000 BCE). The general chronological table on page 1529 groups the Geometric Kebaran under the Epipaleolithic without its own distinctive dates.

p0dkm29sd62.label: Pottery Neolithic
p0dkm29sd62.editorialNote: Based on chronological table on page 1529, this period coincides with part of the post-glacial period of the Ice Age in Europe and the Holocene geological epoch.

p0dkm29msk2.label: Mousterian
p0dkm29msk2.editorialNote: Dates here are site-specific, do not necessarily apply to this period at other sites, and are not made explicit in the general chronological chart on page 1529, which groups Mousterian under Middle Paleolithic. The dates for the Mousterian for the Sharon Plain (140,000-40,000 years BP) differ from these.

p0dkm29zgnh.label: Upper Acheulean
p0dkm29zgnh.editorialNote: Dates here are site-specific and differ from the Acheulean for the Sharon Plain (300,000-150,000 years BP). They do not necessarily correspond to the general chronological table on page 1529, where the Upper Acheulean is encompassed by the Lower Paleolithic.

p0dkm29pb75.label: Late Bronze Age
p0dkm29pb75.editorialNote: This period differs from the general, non-site-specific period given in the chronological table on page 1529, where the Late Bronze Age subdivisions cover 1600-1200 BCE.

p0dkm29jj7s.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0dkm29jj7s.editorialNote: Period corresponds to Abbevillean, Lower and Middle Acheulean, and Upper Acheulean cultural periods; Mindel, Mindel-Riss, and Riss periods in the Ice Age in Europe; the Middle Pleistocene (Quaternary) geological epoch. (derived from chronological table on page 1529)

source.title: Time and its adversaries in the Seleucid empire.

p0b3hfgbbt3.label: The Seleucid Era
p0b3hfgbbt3.editorialNote: Inferred from the following discussions: page 30 states that Seleucus I declared the official Year 1 of the Seleucid Era to be 311 BCE; Figure 1 on page 6 indicates the final Seleucid king, Philip II Barypous, ended his reign in 64 BCE; and page 234 explicitly states the dissolution of the Seleukid kingdom by Pompey in 64 BCE.

p0b3hfggwbx.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 1
p0b3hfggwbx.editorialNote: Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 1: From the death of Alexander the great in 323 BCE to Antigonus Monophthalmus' expulsion of Seleucus Nicator from Babylon in 316 BCE, records were dated by the years of king Philip III Arrhidaeus and then, after his posthumous eighth year, by the years of king Alexander IV;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically.

p0b3hfg9zxd.label: Yona Era
p0b3hfg9zxd.editorialNote: Derived from discussion on p. 99 and accompanying footnote 140: "It is possible that Antimachus I's newly inaugurated dating system is what was later known as the Yona or Yavana (Greek) Era, with an epoch of 175/174 BC; this Greek Era was employed with its Macedonian calendar to north and south of the Hindu Kush into the second century CE [Note 140: It was employed in its 279th year at Surkh Kotal (SK2) and Dasht-e Nawur (DN1=IEOG 319a) by the Kushan King, the grandfather of Kanishka I... Vima Taktu.]"

p0b3hfgg93g.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 2
p0b3hfgg93g.editorialNote: Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 2: From late 316 to 311 BCE, the preiod of Antigonus Monophthalmus's undisputed dominance in Babylonia and Seleucus's exile in Ptolemy's Egypt, records were no longer dated by the reigning monarch, Alexander IV, who was absent in Macedonia. Instead, scribes introduced a year count of Antigonus in his official capacity as lúrab uqu, the Akkadian term for the Greek title stratêgos (general) of Asia....The beginning of this count, in an important precedent for the Seleucid Era, was retrojected to 317/316 BCE;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically.

p0b3hfg99rz.label: Demetrius II Nicator (First Reign)
p0b3hfg99rz.editorialNote: Derived from Figure 1 ("The House of Seleucus, simplified") on page 6, which lays out the genealogy of the Seleucid kings. Demetrius II Nicator reigned twice, with other claimants forcing him out of power in between.

p0b3hfg33km.label: Demetrius II Nicator (Second Reign)
p0b3hfg33km.editorialNote: Derived from Figure 1 ("The House of Seleucus, simplified") on page 6, which lays out the genealogy of the Seleucid kings. Demetrius II Nicator reigned twice, with other claimants forcing him out of power in between.

stop.label: The Middle of the 2nd Century BCE

p0b3hfgnsmn.label: High Seleucid Empire
p0b3hfgnsmn.editorialNote: Derived from the discussion on page 189: "It may be helpful to distinguish...the high Seleucid empire from the third to the middle of the second century BCE...."

p0b3hfg238q.label: Seleucus I Nicator
p0b3hfg238q.editorialNote: Derived from Figure 1 on page 6, as well as discussion on pp. 21-22: "Its [i.e. the Seleucid Empire's] epoch, or Year 1, was placed in 312/311 BCE, six year before Seleucus I took the diadem and proclaimed himself king....At Seleucus I's death in 281 BCE...."

p0b3hfgv457.label: Neo-Babylonian Empire
p0b3hfgv457.editorialNote: Derived from discussion on page 9: "Babylonia...had formed the core of the Neo-Babylonian empire from its foundation by Nabopolassar in the 620s BCE through its expansion under Nebuchadnezzar II in the first decades of the sixth century down to the defeat of Nabonidus and his son Belshazzar by Cyrus the Great in 539 BCE."

p0b3hfg45kc.label: Year-Date Formulae at Babylon Stage 3
p0b3hfg45kc.editorialNote: Derived from the discussion on p. 28: "Stage 3: Following Seleucus Nicator's return to Babylon in 311 BCE, the interrupted regnal count of Alexander IV was restored. Thus, year 7 of general Antigonus was renamed year 6 of Alexander IV. The count was continued even after the young king's murder in 310 BCE. Seleucus's name and the title lúrab uqu, previously used for Antigonus, were added to the regnal year date of Alexander IV, thereby combining features of the stage 1 and stage 2 formulae;" as well as from Table 2 on p. 29, which presents the same information schematically.
