p0jhchf.editorialNote: Chapter from an edited volume; WorldCat URL is for the volume as a whole. The authors state on p. 41 that they will use "the time periods originally proposed by Hafsten (1961)", citing U. Hafsten, 1961, "Pleistocene development of vegetation and climate in the southern high plains as evidence by pollen analysis", in: Wendorf., F. (ed.), Paleoecology of the Llano Estacado, Fort Burgwin Research Center, I, Museum of New Mexico Press, Santa Fe, New Mexico: 59-91.

p07fthdqd8t.label: Paleoindian period
p07fthdqd8t.note: "In this discussion, because the fundamental criteria for defining “Paleoindians” (best articulated in Wormington’s proposed concept of a Paleoeastern Tradition [1957]) as nomadic big-game hunters are being challenged, the Paleoindian period is defined as a temporal span from ca. 11,500 to 8800 years B.P." (p. 116).

p07fthd7n9t.label: Early Paleoindian
p07fthd7n9t.note: On material from Horn Shelter no. 2: "For Fig. 3.9a I have tentatively regarded this material as transitional, between Early and Late Paleoindian; future work or new finds will help clarify the picture" (p. 118).
p07fthd7n9t.editorialNote: Start date from start of Paleoindian; end from chart on p. 113 and explanation of Horn Shelter no. 2 dating on p. 118.

p07fthdrsfd.label: Late Paleoindian
p07fthdrsfd.note: "The subperiod here called Late Paleoindian is in many ways archeologically intermediate (or “transitional”) between Early Paleoindian and the Archaic; the question to be answered is how accurately this material culture–based impression reflects their respective human adaptations" (p. 118).

p07fthdxxsh.label: Archaic
p07fthdxxsh.note: "In briefly reviewing the Archaic of central Texas, the cultural chronological framework proposed by L. Johnson and Goode (1994) is adopted with minor adjustments" (p. 119).

p07fthd99mc.label: Late Prehistoric
p07fthd99mc.note: "Archeologists working in central Texas have not been able to clearly interpret the extent and importance of the material cultural change that occurred in the region ca. 1200 B.P. This is the somewhat arbitrary break commonly made between the long Archaic period and its successor, the Late Prehistoric. Previously this was referred to as the “Neo-American Stage” (D. Suhm et al. 1954, 20) in the expectation that all three defining traits (pottery, bow and arrow, and agriculture) would eventually be recognized. It now appears that generally for central Texas, only the bow and arrow appeared initially, pottery was added later, and agriculture (or, at least, the possession of tropical cultigens) came last and was of quite minor importance. Because basic hunting and gathering subsistence continued, what is here called the Late Prehistoric has also been labeled the “Neo-Archaic” (Prewitt 1981) or the “Post-Archaic” (L. Johnson and Goode 1994). Two subperiods, early and late (see Fig. 3.9), are here recognized in the Late Prehistoric (Jelks 1962); these correspond to the Austin and Toyah “phases” (I will continue to use the term “interval”) of long standing use in the systematics of the local prehistory (Prewitt 1981). More than projectile point style change distinguishes Austin from Toyah manifestations, and the subperiod level of designation is intended to reflect the importance of these differences. I agree with L. Johnson and Goode (1994, 39– 40) when they note that an equally satisfactory solution would be to place the break between the Archaic and the Late Prehistoric at ca. 800 B.P., when Toyah replaces Austin as the prevailing archeological configuration" (p. 122).

p07fthdvbjk.label: Historic Period
p07fthdvbjk.note: "I consider three subperiods in the Historic period of central Texas—early, middle, and late. In the first two, vestiges of both indigenous and European peoples and cultures are represented; in the third, the indigenous peoples have virtually disappeared" (p 123). "The early Historic subperiod in central Texas begins in the late seventeenth century with the first documented arrival of Europeans... The late Historic subperiod, extending into the twentieth century, encompasses minor numbers of mission Indians, farflung nomadic native groups (primarily the Comanches) until the late nineteenth century, and a rich archeological record of the European-derived cultural presence (D. Fox 1983)" (pp. 123-124).
p07fthdvbjk.editorialNote: 1950 is taken as the conventional "present" for B.P. dating systems, and thus the end point for the final "Historic" period.

p07fthdjbz5.label: Early Archaic
p07fthdjbz5.note: "The early part of the Archaic, from ca. 8800 to 6000 B.P., is here subdivided into the three projectile point style intervals: Angostura (see Fig. 3.13b), early split-stem (see Fig. 3.13e, f ), and Martindale- Uvalde (see Fig. 3.13g–k) (see also Fig. 3.9a)" (p. 119).
p07fthdjbz5.editorialNote: Because their chronological boundaries are not clearly noted or obvious from the chronological chart, the style intervals for the Early Archaic have not been included, though the chart breaks seem to fall evenly at 8000 and 7000 B.P.

p07fthdjd2x.label: Middle Archaic
p07fthdjd2x.note: "The middle subperiod of the Archaic, from ca. 6000 to 4000 B.P., too, is further subdivided into three style intervals: Bell-Andice-Calf Creek, Taylor, and Nolan-Travis (see Figs. 3.9a and 3.14b–g)" (p. 120).
p07fthdjd2x.editorialNote: Because the chronological boundaries of the style intervals are not explicitly defined in the text and not clearly noted in the chart on p. 113, they have not been included, although again the chart breaks seem to fall at the round numbers of 5000 B.P. and 4500 B.P.

p07fthdnmw9.label: Late Archaic
p07fthdnmw9.note: "The Late Archaic, ca. 4000 to 1300 or 1200 B.P., began as effective moisture was at its lowest in central Texas, but gradually the climate became substantially more mesic (see Fig. 3.9b). Six style intervals have been postulated for the Late Archaic (see Fig. 3.9a)" (p. 121).
p07fthdnmw9.editorialNote: Because the chronology of the style intervals is not explicit from the chart on p. 113 or described in the text, they have not been included, though in the chart Bulverde and Pedernales/Kinney seem to be placed roundly between 4000 and 2500, with the other four between 2500 and 1200.

p07fthd27hd.label: Early Late Prehistoric
p07fthd27hd.note: "Two subperiods, early and late (see Fig. 3.9), are here recognized in the Late Prehistoric (Jelks 1962); these correspond to the Austin and Toyah “phases” (I will continue to use the term “interval”) of long-standing use in the systematics of the local prehistory (Prewitt 1981)... The most apparent change seen at the beginning of the early Late Prehistoric (or Austin interval) is from a prevalence of dart points to that of arrow points and, inferentially, from use of the atlatl and dart to that of the bow and arrow (see Fig. 3.16c)" (p. 122).
p07fthd27hd.editorialNote: While the text provides "ca. 800 B.P." as the break between the Austin and Toyah intervals (p. 122), the chart on p. 113 -- without offering clear dates -- suggests a date more on the order of 650 B.P.

p07fthdht9w.label: Late Late Prehistoric
p07fthdht9w.note: "The late subperiod of the Late Prehistoric is expressed as a single style interval, designated on Fig. 3.9a by the Perdiz arrow point (see Fig. 3.16f, g)" (p. 123).
p07fthdht9w.editorialNote: Start dates follow the same logic as the end dates of the early Late Prehistoric: 800 B.P. from the break between Austin and Toyah phases mentioned in the text, 650 B.P. inferred from the chart on p. 113. For the end date, initially the text states "The early Historic subperiod in central Texas begins in the late seventeenth century with the first documented arrival of Europeans" (p 123), but subsequently provides the absolute date of 1690, which has been used here.

p07fthdjjrw.label: Early Historic
p07fthdjjrw.note: "The early Historic subperiod in central Texas begins in the late seventeenth century with the first documented arrival of Europeans... Concerted ethnohistorical research (see multiple entries by T. N. Campbell under Indian group names in Branda 1976; Campbell 1988; Hester 1989a, 1989b; Newcomb 1961, 1993) has been used to piece together important yet incomplete accounts that reveal several distinctive features of native cultures in central Texas between ca. 1690 and 1720" (p. 123); "The middle Historic subperiod, when much of the record on aboriginal peoples is in reference to remnants of native groups living in the Spanish missions, began in about 1730 and ended in about 1800 as the mission system was failing (Hester 1989a, 1989b)" (p. 124).
p07fthdjjrw.editorialNote: Note the disjunction between the stated end of the early Historic subperiod and the stated beginning of the middle Historic subperiod.

p07fthdrw64.label: Middle Historic
p07fthdrw64.note: "The middle Historic subperiod, when much of the record on aboriginal peoples is in reference to remnants of native groups living in the Spanish missions, began in about 1730 and ended in about 1800 as the mission system was failing (Hester 1989a, 1989b)" (p. 124).

p07fthdfh68.label: Late Historic
p07fthdfh68.note: "The late Historic subperiod, extending into the twentieth century, encompasses minor numbers of mission Indians, farflung nomadic native groups (primarily the Comanches) until the late nineteenth century, and a rich archeological record of the European-derived cultural presence (D. Fox 1983). As the Comanche presence in central Texas waned in the mid to late nineteenth century, more than eleven millennia of Native American presence in the area came to an end" (p. 124).
p07fthdfh68.editorialNote: The end range for this period balances the textual assertion that the period ended in the mid to late 19th century, the textual assertion that it extended into the 20th century, and the chart, which seems to let it run up to 0 B.P. (1950).

source.citation: Collins, M.B. 2004. “Archeology in Central Texas.” In The Prehistory of Texas, edited by Timothy K. Perttula, 101–126. Texas A&M Anthropology Series 9. College Station, TX: Texas A&M University Press.
source.title: Archeology in Central Texas

p07fthd.editorialNote: The citation is to a chapter in an edited volume; the WorldCat link is to the record for the volume as a whole. The chapter appears to be an almost verbatim reproduction of Collins, M.B. 1995. “Forty years of archeology in Central Texas.” Bulletin of the Texas Archeological Society 66: 361–400, and should be considered interchangeable with Collins 1995.

p0t3585v34n.label: Dry Edwards Interval
p0t3585v34n.editorialNote: The start dates for the period are inferred from the chart on p. 5, where the beginning of the Dry Edwards Interval seems to be marked at ca. 3000 B.C., and from text on p. 31: "Closer to the Gulf coast, the Columbus Bend formation of the lower Colorado River is composed of several alluvial members of interest. According to sometimes ambiguous radiocarbon assays for West Point and Columbus, Member 1 appears to have stopped its growth and become stable sometime between 3200 B.C. and 2500 B.C. (Blum 1992:156, 175-178, 189). In actuality, the indicated dry period almost certainly corresponds to the Edwards Interval"; "For the Medina, I would date this cessation of flooding, which is surely a dryness indicator, to sometime between 2700 B.C. and 2300 B.C., judging from the available radiocarbon assays (Thorns and Mandel 1992)". The end dates are provided by the chart on p. 5, where the curve returns to mesic conditions at approximately the 600 B.C. mark, and by the text on p. 15, where correlations between stratigraphy at Fort Hood and the Jonas Terrace site show that "The growth of Stratum 4 and Member D1 ceased about 600 or 500 B.C., according to the charcoal dates, and shortly thereafter floodplain/terrace aggradation commenced once more, creating alluvial Stratum 3 at Jonas Terrace and alluvial Member D2 at Fort Hood."

p0t3585b2rd.label: Paleoindian Era
p0t3585b2rd.editorialNote: The chart on p. 5 simply provides dotted lines with no upper limit for this period; the start date range here is derived from the earliest calibrated radiocarbon date on p. 8 and the beginning date of the chart; the end date is provided by the reference to the start of the Early Archaic period on p. 21.

p0t3585kxnj.label: Archaic Era
p0t3585kxnj.note: "The Early Archaic period of the Plateau, in some places beginning around 6500 B.C. or earlier, as at the Wilson-Leonard site (41WM235), represents almost three millennia when bison were supposedly absent from the region (cf. Dillehay 1974)" (p.20); "I provisionally stop the Late Archaic period around A.D. 600... Nevertheless, one should underscore the fact that some cultural and considerable economic continuity tied the end of the Late Archaic period with what came directly afterwards. In fact, of all the period boundaries set in the present paper, that for the ending of the Late Archaic II subperiod is the most subjective and bothersome... If the informed reader wishes to terminate the Late Archaic period at A.D. 1200, I will not argue. Or if the reader wants to stop the period at around A.D. 400 (or later), when very small "dart" points of the Darl and Figueroa sort appear in the region, that is another possibility" (pp. 39-40).
p0t3585kxnj.editorialNote: Temporal coverage takes start from start of first subperiod, end from end of last subperiod; the label and the period-subperiod relationship is drawn from the chart on p. 5.

p0t3585fjns.label: Post-Archaic Era
p0t3585fjns.note: "I provisionally stop the Late Archaic period around A.D. 600...Nevertheless, one should underscore the fact that some cultural and considerable economic continuity tied the end of the Late Archaic period with what came directly afterwards. In fact, of all the period boundaries set in the present paper, that for the ending of the Late Archaic II subperiod is the most subjective and bothersome. For one thing, human culture did not change greatly after the beginning of that interval down through the days when Scallorn arrowheads were in vogue. If the informed reader wishes to terminate the Late Archaic period at A.D. 1200, I will not argue. Or if the reader wants to stop the period at around A.D. 400 (or later), when very small "dart" points of the Darl and Figueroa sort appear in the region, that is another possibility" (pp. 39-40). "The present historical narrative concludes at A.D. 1600, near the end of Toyah days when Perdiz arrowheads were in vogue" (p. 41).
p0t3585fjns.editorialNote: While the author indicates that the Late Archaic period ends around A.D. 600 in the chart on p. 5 and in the text on p. 39, the subsequent expressions about alternatives and uncertainties are represented by the A.D. 400-1200 range. The author indicates a preference for the label "Post-Archaic" on p. 18, where it is attributed to Prewitt in an unpublished report, but all of the cited works by Prewitt in fact use "Neoarchaic".

p0t35856b5j.label: Early Archaic Period
p0t35856b5j.editorialNote: End date for period taken from chart on p. 5 and from start date of following period.

p0t3585nqbr.label: Middle Archaic Period
p0t3585nqbr.note: "The short Middle Archaic period of some 1300 years commences around 3600 B.C. and can best be taken as a transitional epoch" (p. 24).

p0t3585c8d7.label: Late Archaic Period
p0t3585c8d7.note: "I provisionally stop the Late Archaic period around A.D. 600... Nevertheless, one should underscore the fact that some cultural and considerable economic continuity tied the end of the Late Archaic period with what came directly afterwards. In fact, of all the period boundaries set in the present paper, that for the ending of the Late Archaic II subperiod is the most subjective and bothersome... If the informed reader wishes to terminate the Late Archaic period at A.D. 1200, I will not argue. Or if the reader wants to stop the period at around A.D. 400 (or later), when very small "dart" points of the Darl and Figueroa sort appear in the region, that is another possibility" (pp. 39-40).

p0t3585t8hz.label: Late Archaic I
p0t3585t8hz.note: "However dry the climate of the Edwards Interval, Part I of the Late Archaic period (2300 B.C. to 600 B.C.) witnessed no hardships for the aborigines, who apparently came to thrive on upland semi-succulents" (p. 34).

p0t35858nxt.label: Late Archaic II
p0t35858nxt.note: "In the Late Archaic II subperiod (largely corresponding to the Middle Woodland in eastern North America), which lasted from 600 B.C. to A.D. 600, fairly mesic conditions had returned to all but the western and southwestern parts of the Edwards Plateau" (p. 36).
p0t35858nxt.editorialNote: While the broader Archaic and Late Archaic periods have a broader end range, and while the author expresses uncertainty about the end date of Late Archaic II, the central definition on p. 36 uses A.D. 600 unequivocally as the end date.

source.citation: Johnson, L., and G.T. Goode. 1994. “A new try at dating and characterizing Holocene climates, as well as archeological periods, on the eastern Edwards Plateau.” Bulletin of the Texas Archeological Society 65: 1–55.
source.title: A New Try at Dating and Characterizing Holocene Climates, as well as Archeological Periods, on the Eastern Edwards Plateau

p08vvjkjsgg.label: Early Byzantine
p08vvjkjsgg.note: "The first golden age of the empire, the Early Byzantine period, extends from the founding of the new capital into the 700s."

p08vvjkcfqt.label: Middle Byzantine
p08vvjkcfqt.note:
"The resolution of the Iconoclastic controversy in favor of the use of icons
ushered in a second flowering of the empire, the Middle Byzantine period (843–1204)."

p08vvjksgbh.label: Latin Occupation
p08vvjksgbh.note: "In 1204, armies of the Fourth Crusade invaded from western Europe, conquering the ancient Byzantine imperial capital and founding the “Latin Empire of Constantinople,” while other imperial territories also fell to Crusader rule. The Crusader state in Constantinople was one of several in the thirteenth-century Levant, all under the spiritual authority of the pope as head of the Latin Church of Western Europe... This Crusader state lasted from 1204 until 1261, when Byzantine rule was reestablished in Constantinople and limited portions of the former Byzantine empire were also retaken. The Latin Occupation of 1204–61 had a profound effect on the empire and the Byzantine peoples, causing major political fragmentation as well as the dislocation of Byzantine populations, especially the empire’s nobility and ruling classes."

p08vvjkdcnx.label: Late Byzantium
p08vvjkdcnx.note: "The focus of Byzantine power was now centered in Constantinople, and extended westward to northern and central Greece, and south into the Peloponnesos. In the east, the Byzantine Empire of Trebizond, which had flourished during the Latin Occupation, continued to exist as an independently ruled Byzantine territory in competition with the Palaiologan-ruled empire with its capital at Constantinople. The last Byzantine lands would be conquered by the Ottoman Turks in the mid-fifteenth century, with Constantinople taken in 1453, and Mistra and Trebizond in 1460."

p08vvjk5t32.label: Byzantium
p08vvjk5t32.editorialNote: Period term derived from the heading of the essay on Byzantine culture and chronology.

source.citation: S. Brooks. 2001-2009. "The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)." New York: The Metropolitan Museum of Art. https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/byza/hd_byza.htm.
source.title: The Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)

p08vvjk.editorialNote: Page notes "originally published October 2001, last revised October 2009". This authority represents an essay in the larger Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, general editors Elizabeth Weinfield and Philomena Mariani.

p0nt759mt2t.label: Позднеантичный
p0nt759mt2t.note:
"В третьей четверти III в. начинается заключительный этап римского периода в истории Херсонеса, который иногда рассматривают в качестве самостоятельного и называют позднеантичным. Его начало относится к третьей четверти III, а конец - ко второй четверти - середине VI в."

English version: "The third quarter of the 3rd century AD marked the final stage of the Roman period in the history of Chersonesos, a period which is sometimes considered a separate phase and called Late Antiquity. It begins in the third quarter of the 3rd century AD and ends in the mid-third quarter of the 6th century AD."
p0nt759mt2t.editorialNote: The spatial coverage of this period extends to the site of Tauric Chersonesos (https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/226564) in Crimea, but spatial coverage area cannot be specified because Crimea is currently considered occupied territory by the international community (Ukrainian sovereignty, Russian control).

p0nt759xcps.label: Римский

stop.label: не позднее третьей четверти III в.

p0nt759xcps.note:
"Вследствие этого, в середине 60-х гг. I в. н.э., легат римской провинции Мезии Тиберий Плавтий Сильван пришел на помощь Херсонесу и разгромил угрожавших городу варваров. После этого римские власти стали более активно вмешиваться во внутренние дела Херсонеса, что отразилось на чеканке монеты... Около 250 г. римские войска вновь появляются в Крыму, но, судя по имеющимся сейчас данным, они теперь дислоцировались уже только в Херсонесе и, следовательно, масштабы римского военного присутствия в сравнении с более ранним временем сократились. Но на этот раз римские войска здесь оставались недолго и были выведены не позднее третьей четверти III в. Этим заканчивается более чем столетняя история постоянного римского военного присутствия в Таврике."

English version: "In the mid-60s AD the legate of the Roman province of Moesia, Tiberius Plautius Silvanus, aided Chersonesos in defeating the barbarians who were threatening the city. After these events the Roman authorities started to intervene in the internal politics of Chersonesos more forcefully, a circumstance which was reflected in the issue of coinage... In approximately 250 AD Roman troops appeared in Crimea again, but were stationed only in Chersonesos so that the scale of the Roman presence was smaller in comparison with the earlier period. This time the Romans stayed in Chersonesos for a shorter period and finally left in the third quarter of the 3rd century."
p0nt759xcps.editorialNote: The spatial coverage of this period extends to the site of Tauric Chersonesos (https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/226564) in Crimea, but spatial coverage area cannot be specified because Crimea is currently considered occupied territory by the international community (Ukrainian sovereignty, Russian control).

p0nt759pz84.label: Средневековый
p0nt759pz84.note:
"После разделения Великой Римской империи на Западную и Восточную Херсон (сокращенная форма названия города окончательно вытеснила старое приблизительно к концу VI в.) становится одним из пограничных рубежей Византийской империи и на протяжении всего средневекового периода остается главным форпостом Византии в Северном Причерноморье... В 1399 году Херсон был разрушен татарами окончательно и на месте некогда процветавшего города остались уже никогда не возродившиеся руины, и последний рукоположенный в 1440 году митрополит Херсона, жил уже не в городе, а где-то в окрестностях."

English version: "After the division of the Roman empire into the Western and Eastern empires Cherson (this shortened form replaced the ancient name of the city approximately at the end of the 6th century) became one of the frontier regions of Byzantium. During the entire medieval period it served as the major Byzantine outpost in the northern Black Sea region... In 1399 the Tatars finally destroyed Cherson, so that only ruins remained where once stood a prosperous city. The last metropolitan of Cherson was appointed in 1440 and lived in the outskirts of town."
p0nt759pz84.editorialNote: The spatial coverage of this period extends to the site of Tauric Chersonesos (https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/226564) in Crimea, but spatial coverage area cannot be specified because Crimea is currently considered occupied territory by the international community (Ukrainian sovereignty, Russian control).

source.citation: Project "Megarica". 2016. http://chersonesos.org.
source.title: Chersonesos.org

p0b6j5mmfbc.label: Byzantine
p0b6j5mmfbc.note: Metropolitan Museum Heilbrunn timeline begins Byzantine history at the foundation of Constatinople (https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/byza/hd_byza.htm); chersonesos.org notes final destruction of Chersonesos by Mongols in 1399.

p0b6j5mmx9p.label: 11th-12th century
p0b6j5mmx9p.note: 11th century understood to begin in the years immediately following the destruction of the site by Vladimir of Kyiv in 988/989 CE.

p0b6j5m3t44.label: 13th century
p0b6j5m3t44.note: Broad designation derived from pottery chronology and from the stratigraphic history of the site (final period of occupation), independent of historical/art-historical periodization (hence the start at 1200 rather than with the Fourth Crusade and the capture of Constantinople in 1204). Used for the final phase of occupation in the South Region, which seems to have been destroyed before the end of the 13th century and largely abandoned.

p0b6j5mtpfd.label: Early Byzantine (5th-7th century)
p0b6j5mtpfd.note: This period definition reflects common usage, pottery chronologies, and site stratification at Chersonesos, starting later than the Metropolitan Museum Heilbrunn timeline and stopping before the period of iconoclasm noted as "the 700s" in the Heilbrunn timeline.

p0b6j5mq3ms.label: Middle Byzantine (9th-11th century)
p0b6j5mq3ms.note: Conventionally, this period starts with the end of Iconoclasm in 843 CE, but this definition is based on pottery chronologies and is more general in its start date. The end date is the conventional end of the period with the capture of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade and the beginning of the period of Latin control.

p0b6j5mzmnj.label: Late Byzantine (13th-14th century)
p0b6j5mzmnj.note: From the Latin conquest of Constantinople to the historical date for the final sack of Chersonesos.

p0b6j5mgvqt.label: Hellenistic
p0b6j5mgvqt.note: Start date reflects beginning of floruit of Greek city; end date provided by the historical dates for the firm inclusion of Chersonesos into the Roman orbit.

p0b6j5mh84m.label: Roman
p0b6j5mh84m.note: Start date provided by chersonesos.org, which notes that the city's close alliance with Romans starts in "mid 60s" of the 1st century CE.

p0b6j5m46gm.label: Modern
p0b6j5m46gm.note: Start date provided by the foundation of Sevastopol in 1783; end date provided by the final season of excavation in the South Region.

p0b6j5m239w.label: Late Antique
p0b6j5m239w.note: This period was not originally applied in the South Region excavations, where this range was covered by a loose intersection between the "Roman" and "Early Byzantine" periods.

p0b6j5mh78j.label: Iconoclasm
p0b6j5mh78j.note: This period is only obliquely referenced in the Metropolitan Museum Heilbrunn Timeline as "the Iconoclastic controversy", which occupies the "700s and early 800s". Wikipedia has a more precise definition for the period of Iconoclasm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Iconoclasm), and divides it into two periods: 730-787 CE and 814-843. The history of the site provided at chersonesos.org notes that Chersonesos was made a thematic capital in 841 CE, so this may be a more natural end date for its "Dark Ages" (a term now deprecated).

p0b6j5mq68m.label: Early Hellenistic
p0b6j5mq68m.note: Period runs more or less from the beginning to the end of the amphora-stamp series for Chersonesos amphorae; the 270/260 BCE date is also derived from the note at chersonesos.org that this is the period at which the Scythian incursions into the territory of Chersonesos begin.

p0b6j5mv5hb.label: Middle Hellenistic
p0b6j5mv5hb.note: From the beginning of the wars with the Scythians to the appointment of Diophantes by Mithridates, according to http://chersonesos.org.

p0b6j5md9jr.label: Late Hellenistic
p0b6j5md9jr.note: Period of growing intervention by the Romans at Chersonesos, according to http://chersonesos.org.

p0b6j5m3c4q.label: 12th to mid-13th century
p0b6j5m3c4q.note: Period term used to describe stratigraphic deposits and objects that date broadly to the last two phases of activity in the South Region of Chersonesos, but that cannot be dated specifically to the final phase. This includes objects that were found in the destruction layers but may have been created decades beforehand. The stop year range is a terminus ante quem defined by the earliest date at which we think the destruction of the South Region might have taken place and the latest reasonable date that matches our evidence for the near-total destruction of the city in the 13th century (the material suggests that a date previously proposed to match historical records of an incursion by Nogay Khan in 1299 is too late).

source.citation: A. Rabinowitz and L. Sedikova. 2020. Chersonesos South Region Periodization.
source.title: Chersonesos South Region Periodization

p0b6j5m.editorialNote: Periodization developed in the course of excavations carried out by the joint Institute of Classical Archaeology (University of Texas)/National Preserve of Tauric Chersonesos project in the South Region of Chersonesos in Crimea from 2001-2006, refined for database implementation and final publication between 2008 and 2020.

source.title: AMCR Periods Vocabulary

creators.name: Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic

source.citation: Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) Periods Vocabulary
source.locator: Locator provided for each term is the ID used for referencing the term in the original database.

p0s2rwkc5hz.label: Historic
p0s2rwkc5hz.note: General term for later phases of complex civilizations

p0s2rwkf8h7.label: Smithfield
p0s2rwkf8h7.note: Smithfield used specifically without a following letter designation includes assemblages with backed bladelets, long end scrapers at end of sequence from Karoo.

p0s2rwkk4mx.label: Ceramic Wilton
p0s2rwkk4mx.note: Wilton, probably hunter-gatherers, but with pottery

p0s2rwk49st.label: Herder
p0s2rwk49st.note: Herders are pastoralists with fat-tailed sheep, cows and Khoekhoe pottery

p0s2rwkqncn.label: Strandloper
p0s2rwkqncn.note: coastally adapted hunter-gatherers with few formal tools, large untrimmed flakes

p0s2rwkdxrz.label: LSA
p0s2rwkdxrz.note:
ArchStrat LSA includes those assemblages that are of non-specific LSA attribution.

Only use this ArchStrat if you have no further information.

p0s2rwkrbhq.label: Iron Age
p0s2rwkrbhq.note: Farming societies, agriculturalists with metal, animals, farming, generally defined

p0s2rwkzmr7.label: Post-Wilton
p0s2rwkzmr7.note:
Small hafted scrapers, associated with backed bladelets but few to no segments, younger than Wilton.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town.

p0s2rwkjb3t.label: Smithfield N
p0s2rwkjb3t.note: concave scrapers for wood working, from Natal (N)

p0s2rwk492m.label: Smithfield P
p0s2rwk492m.note: small hafted straight-sided scrapers with steep retouch for wood working, from Pongoland (P)

p0s2rwkqqsq.label: Smithfield General
p0s2rwkqqsq.note:
Smithfield, with no clarification, was used before the time when Smithfield was divided into sub-divisions (A, B, C).

Smithfield without a clear definition of time.

p0s2rwkb59z.label: Indian Microlithic
p0s2rwkb59z.note:
Sites with microlithic technologies including backed pieces, microblades, microblade cores. In India the definition of microlithic begins at length of 3 cm (width not defined).

Age range based on max age for Mehtakheri and general min age for late hunter gatherers. Often the younger appearance of microlithic cultures is termed Mesolithic in India but we do not differentiate these in ROAD.
p0s2rwkb59z.editorialNote: Label adjusted to "Indian Microlithic" as of June 2024.

p0s2rwkwbsz.label: Bronze Age
p0s2rwkwbsz.note: Approximate beginning of the Bronze Age in Levant, through the beginning of the Iron Age in the Hittite Empire.

p0s2rwkdztt.label: Wilton
p0s2rwkdztt.note:
Long and narrow scrapers for leather working, associated with backed bladelets but not segments.

Classic Wilton, microlithic assemblage with high incidence of backed bladelets and especially segments or crescents, borers, small scrapers on truncated flakes and blades, oval double scrapers with steep retouch along both margins (= double segments), ornaments, polished bone tools.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town.

See Lombard et al. 2012 for age.

p0s2rwkkkxz.label: Neolithic
p0s2rwkkkxz.note: Early farming societies, dates based on early start in Levant and late end in Europe.

p0s2rwksqkd.label: Albany
p0s2rwksqkd.note:
Albany and Oakhurst assemblages contain few or no microliths, scrapers (round end, D-shaped, duckbill), polished bone tools.

Lockshoek is the Karoo variant.

Smithfield A: large round or rectangular scrapers > 30mm for leather working.

Based on Deacon HJ, Deacon J, 1999. Human Beginnings in South Africa. David Philip Publishers, Cape Town.

See Lombard et al. 2012 for age.

p0s2rwkg7bp.label: Late Acacus
p0s2rwkg7bp.note: Late Acacus characterized by groups with diversified extractive economy, almost exclusive mountain environment settlement pattern and semi-residential occupation. These indicate a reduced mobility and a more intensive exploitation of the local environment, in comparatively more arid conditions, starting ca. 8500 BP (Vernet AAR 2003 review of Garcea 2001).

p0s2rwkgggp.label: Early Acacus
p0s2rwkgggp.note: Early Acacus characterized by specialized extractive economy, dual settlement pattern (mountains and ergs), and high level of mobility. This system required exploitation of resources over a wide territory. However, no cereal pollen types were recovered in Early Acacus deposits (Vernet AAR 2003 review of Garcea 2001).

p0s2rwk4tvb.label: Oranian
p0s2rwk4tvb.note: Eastern Oranian 14000-10000 in Libya, Final Paleolithic, also called Iberomaurusian

p0s2rwkpzxh.label: Epigravettian
p0s2rwkpzxh.note:
The Epigravettian technocomplex is well known in southern and eastern Europe and dates right after the Gravettian. Its material culture is similar to the Gravettian with the use of fine blades, bladelets, and, in many cases, microblades to manufacture backed tools. Bone tools, art, and symbolic artifacts, mostly representing animals and geometric motives, are also very common.

One site in Armenia, Kalavan-1, is attributed to the Epigravettian, but to date, no Gravettian sites are known from the Caucasus. If it is true it is the southeastern-most occurrence of the Epigravettian.
p0s2rwkpzxh.editorialNote: Coverage changed from "Europe" to "Eurasia" as of June 2024.

p0s2rwks8k2.label: Epipaleolithic
p0s2rwks8k2.note:
Late prehistoric hunter-gatherer societies before the advent of agriculture.

Technically, the Epipaleolithic is defined as the final phase of the Upper Paleolithic. However, we consider the Epipaleolithic as its own category because it falls mainly outside the time range and scope of the ROCEEH project.

p0s2rwkwb33.label: Magosian
p0s2rwkwb33.note: Mixed industry of Middle Stone Age and Later Stone Age artifacts, dates estimated.

p0s2rwkd4n5.label: Harifian
p0s2rwkd4n5.note:
Harif point, obliquely truncated bladelet with pointed base formed by microburin technique and steep retouch. Summary: Microburin technique used habitually on large sites, absent in small inventories, Harif points, small lunates and triangles, Mostly simple backing, Helwan retouch very rare, Round houses.

Found in desert southern Levant, Negev and Sinai, contemporaneous with late Natufian of northern parts of the Levant (Goring-Morris 1987, 257, Schyle & Uerpmann 1996, 268). Harifian hunter-gatherer culture in seasonal camps defined at Abu Salem in Central Negev (Marks & Scott 1976), discovered 1969 around the plateau of Tar Harif.

p0s2rwksjfw.label: Natufian
p0s2rwksjfw.note:
Natufian most widely known Epipalaeolithic industry in Near East, already discovered in the 1920s. Ground stone tools and blades with sickle gloss indicate use and cultivation of cereals. Summary: Use of classical and Krukowski microburin technique, Lunates, size and style Helwan retouch or simple backing, Picks and sickle blades with gloss, Regular use of ground stone tools like mortars, mullers and pestles.

Natufian occurs in central and northern Palestine, with fewer finds in southern Palestine, the steppe of the Negev and Sinai, high Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains, and Syro-Arabian Desert. Microliths and geometrics make up >40% of every assemblage.

p0s2rwkqk3r.label: Robberg
p0s2rwkqk3r.note:
The Robberg industry is characterized by standardized production of bladelets using punch technique. Cores are often worked in bipolar mode (Mitchell 2002: The Archaeology of Southern Africa). Mainly microlithic, few backed tools, few scrapers of variable size, many unretouched bladelets.

Age based on Lombard et al. 2012, could be back to 22,000.

p0s2rwknq95.label: Mushabian
p0s2rwknq95.note:
Classic Mushabian characterized by dominance of arch-backed bladelets, La Mouillah points and scalene triangles, all truncated at one end using microburin technique. Helwan lunates also included. Rectangular and trapezoidal microliths mostly absent. Some assemblages contain Ramon points, similar to La Mouillah points. Summary: Microburin technique, Arch-backed bladelets and scalene triangles, La Mouillah points, all truncated at one end using microburin technique.

The Mushabian was found in southern Jordan, Negev and Sinai and can be divided into an earlier phase (14,500-12,800 BP) of a classical Mushabian and a later phase with the finds from Shunera (Goring-Morris 1987) which overlaps with the Early Natufian (12,800-11,000 BP). It was first discovered during excavations in the northern Sinai in the 1970s (Phillips & Mintz 1977).

p0s2rwkw38q.label: Geometric Kebaran
p0s2rwkw38q.note:
Lithics consist of laminar debitage and microliths, >50% rectangular and trapezoidal forms. Addition of 2nd truncation on Geometric Kebaran blanks, resulting in rectangular microliths unlike truncated pieces of Kebaran. Summary: No habitual use of microburin technique, geometric microliths, Mostly rectangular and trapezoidal forms, Rare occurrence of Helwan retouch, Regular finds of shell beads and ornaments.

Geometric Kebaran or Kebaran A dates 14,500-12,500 BP from southern Sinai to Syria. Older sites are found on the coast and may correlate with dry conditions of the LGM. During more humid conditions until the Geometric Kebaran expanded further inland, ending ca. 13,000 BP before the early Natufian climatic deterioration. Finds from the north in the El Kowm Basin of Syria are quite similar to those from southern Sinai.

p0s2rwk4tpt.label: Iberomaurusian
p0s2rwk4tpt.note:
Small elements like backed bladelets in western North Africa.

Also called Oranian.

p0s2rwkv3zf.label: Magdalenian
p0s2rwkv3zf.note: Blade-dominated industry, rich bone industry, figurative art, many different types of ornaments.

p0s2rwkzvzs.label: Dabban
p0s2rwkzvzs.note: Blade-based industry, endscrapers, burins, backed bladelets, chamfered blades.

p0s2rwkn79h.label: Nizzanian
p0s2rwkn79h.note:
Assemblages are characterized by small triangular microliths, and gravette and microgravette points. Further finds include beautiful end scrapers and dihedral burins. The microburin technique is used habitually. Summary: Habitual use of the microburin technique, Small triangular microliths, gravette points and microgravettes.

Sites of the Nizzanian are often grouped into older phases of Geometric Kebaran dating to 17-15 ka BP and contemporary with later Kebaran. First sites described are Wadi Jilat 6 and Ein Gev IV (Bar-Yosef 1980, 1981). Newer finds have expanded the distribution of the Nizzanian from the Negev and the coastal plains to the Azraq Basin (Garrard 1998). Sites vary considerably in size, from huge expanses in Wadi Jilat 6 and Karaneh IV, to smaller sizes and ephemeral camps.

p0s2rwkrm8q.label: Kebaran
p0s2rwkrm8q.note:
Simple, lacks complexity and abundance of forms compared to later industries. Differences fluid, assemblages dominated by micropoints (curved backed bladelets with wider base), backed points, obliquely truncated backed bladelets, micropoints, or other backed pieces. Summary: No habitual use of the microburin technique, Mostly non-geometric microliths, First industry with invasive retouch/backing of the pieces, Two large phases, with the later phase yielding truncated pieces.

Dates about 20-14 ka uncal BP Fellner (1995a, 22). A widespread phenomenon in the Mediterranean zone and oases of Palestine, Israel, southern Syria, Lebanon and western Jordan, extending into the desert areas of the Negev and Sinai. The desert areas seem to have been settled slightly later, with dates of about 16 ka uncal BP.

p0s2rwkp72n.label: Solutrean
p0s2rwkp72n.note:
Different bifacially retouched tool types, especially leaf points.

Includes Solutrean and also Badegoulian industries.

p0s2rwkdqt2.label: ELSA
p0s2rwkdqt2.note: ELSA is characterised by large scrapers, including circular, convex, concave and informal types, scaled pieces, broad irregular flakes, and micro-blades with predominantly plain striking platforms.

p0s2rwkvbjp.label: Masraqan
p0s2rwkvbjp.note:
Assemblages with finely retouched, elongated bladelets. Blanks narrow, slightly curved, not twisted. Elongated, narrow, single plat cores with intensive prep. Simple end scrapers, burins present. Microburin tech not used. Ambiguous use of backing rare. Summary: Non-geometric microliths, small, partially retouched bladelets, Larger blade tools blades, simple end scrapers, Mostly lat retouch, backing not habitual, No microburin tech, First ground stone tools, rare shell beads, bone tools.

The Masraqan is a term for sites also labeled late Ahmarian, late Upper Paleolithic, Terminal Upper Paleolithic, Proto-Kebaran and even Kebaran. The sites range from the Sinai and Negev, to Jordan and further north to Lebanon.

p0s2rwk4546.label: MSA/LSA

en: Middle Stone Age to Later Stone Age Transition

p0s2rwk4546.note:
Transitional phase between Middle Stone Age (MSA) and Later Stone Age (LSA).

Following van Riet Lowe, Clark, Klein, Mitchell, Barham, and others, for vague and diverse industries.

p0s2rwkkmk9.label: Nebekian
p0s2rwkkmk9.note:
Typical tools include finely retouched, elongated, narrow bladelets. Pieces are either arch-backed or obliquely truncated. Bladelets are fragmented due to the microburin technique and represent the oldest examples showing the habitual use of this technique in the Levant. Summary: Elongated backed bladelets, arch-backed bladelets and microliths, First common use of microburin technique (both classical and Krukowski type).

The term Nebekian was first used by Rust (1950) for the artifacts he excavated in Yabroud, Shelter 3, layers 6 and 7. Madamaghan sites in southern Jordan may belong to the Nebekian if the lunates of these inventories are indeed intrusive. The distribution of the Nebekian seems to be towards the eastern steppic region of the Levant, even though the low number of sites makes this assumption diffcult to prove.

p0s2rwk7pr3.label: Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwk7pr3.note: Use this term for Levantine Upper Paleolithic assemblages.

p0s2rwkgtzf.label: Atlitian
p0s2rwkgtzf.note: Upper Palaeolithic assemblage named for the type site, Atlit, in Mount Carmel. There are several layers with Aurignacian-like assemblages and this culture followed the Antelian (formerly Middle Aurignacian). It was among the assemblages that preceded various Mesolithic developments in the Near East. See Copeland 1975 Aurignacian C, last Aurignacian phase, dates estimated.

p0s2rwk9j72.label: Ahmarian
p0s2rwk9j72.note:
Straight blades.

Middle to Upper Paleolithic Transition, Late Ahmarian also known as Masraqan.

p0s2rwk489f.label: Levantine Aurignacian
p0s2rwk489f.note: Carinated forms, blade industry, bone tools.

p0s2rwkgvzp.label: Microlithic LSA
p0s2rwkgvzp.note: Late Pleistocene pre- or aceramic Later Stone Age (LSA) techno-complexes in Central Africa, predating 30,000 BP, microlithic industries on quartz.

p0s2rwk5623.label: MSA 4
p0s2rwk5623.editorialNote: More general term (broader spatiotemporal coverage) than Final MSA (defined at Sibudu Cave including Border Cave).

p0s2rwkpxb7.label: Late Pietersburg
p0s2rwkpxb7.note: Conversation between Michaela Ecker and Lyn Wadley in 2011 defined Late Pieterburg as Final Middle Stone Age and post-Howiesonspoort, for example at Border Cave (Beaumont).

p0s2rwk7np7.label: Post-Still Bay
p0s2rwk7np7.note: Used only at sites with no Howiesonspoort, late Middle Stone Age sites, generally not used.

p0s2rwknqbf.label: MSA
p0s2rwknqbf.note:
ArchStrat Middle Stone Age (MSA) includes those assemblages that are of non-specific MSA attribution.

Only use this ArchStrat if you have no further information.

p0s2rwkzhsq.label: Pietersburg
p0s2rwkzhsq.note:
Includes tools and elongate flakes made on hornfels (see Bushman Rock Shelter, Cave of Hearths, Border Cave), but generally not well defined, Sampson used it for all sites north of Johannesburg.

General Middle Stone Age term for a variety of assemblage types, but sometimes used as synonym for Howiesonspoort, before 1965 Still Bay used for all sites with points, see also Bambata.

p0s2rwkn8cc.label: Aurignacian
p0s2rwkn8cc.note: General Aurignacian techno-complexes from Europe with carinated tools, blade industry, bone tools, figurative art.

p0s2rwkchqc.label: Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkchqc.note:
Sites with prepared core technologies.

The age range is very broad and based on the maximum age for Attirampakkam and the minimum age for Jwalapuram, both in southern India. Together these define the MP of India, which tends to overlap with dates of the LP.

p0s2rwkb67n.label: Final MSA
p0s2rwkb67n.note:
Defined at Sibudu Cave for very latest Middle Stone Age industries dated at 38.6 ka (Jacobs et al. 2008), also includes Border Cave.

Alternate labels based on Wurz S, 2002. Variability in the Middle Stone Age Lithic Sequence, 115,000–60,000 Years Ago at Klasies River, South Africa. Journal of Archaeological Science 29, 1001–1015.
p0s2rwkb67n.editorialNote: More specific term (narrower spatiotemporal coverage) than MSA 4 (defined for Southern Africa more broadly).

p0s2rwk9v36.label: Early Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwk9v36.note: General Early Upper Paleolithic techno-complexes from Eurasia.

p0s2rwkdmx5.label: Proto-Aurignacian
p0s2rwkdmx5.note:
Many (often retouched) bladelets.

Sometimes called Archaic Aurignacian, with the type site as Fumane Cave in Italy.

p0s2rwkfvcf.label: Post-Howiesonspoort
p0s2rwkfvcf.note:
Defined at Sibudu Cave for MSA industries after HP dated at 58.5 ka (Jacobs et al. 2008), also includes Border Cave and expanded to include younger assemblages after HP without specific dating.

Alternate labels based on Wurz S, 2002. Variability in the Middle Stone Age Lithic Sequence, 115,000–60,000 Years Ago at Klasies River, South Africa. Journal of Archaeological Science 29, 1001–1015.
p0s2rwkfvcf.editorialNote: More general term (broader spatiotemporal coverage) than MSA 3 (defined at Sibudu Cave including Border Cave).

p0s2rwkhqmw.label: Uluzzian
p0s2rwkhqmw.note:
Early Upper Paleolithic technocomplex focusing on flake production. Frequent use of bipolar technique and high frequency of splintered pieces. Several retouched backed pieces, sometimes classifiable as “lunates”.

Minimum age is based on Campanian ignimbrite (39300).

p0s2rwktzs7.label: Chatelperronian
p0s2rwktzs7.note:
Backed points.

For now, we still consider Chatelperronian as Middle Paleolithic, dating subject to change.

p0s2rwktxzf.label: Emiran
p0s2rwktxzf.note:
Emireh points with base tapered by means of bifacial retouch.

Middle to Upper Paleolithic Transition, also Emiran.

p0s2rwkrq2q.label: Initial Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwkrq2q.note:
Earliest Upper Paleolithic in Eurasia.

Middle Paleolithic to Upper Paleolithic transitional industry, e.g., Emiran.

p0s2rwkgr7p.label: Denticulate Mousterian
p0s2rwkgr7p.note:
Levallois technology, many denticulates.

Based on late appearance of denticulates in many French sequences, but could be older.

p0s2rwkbdx5.label: Late Mousterian
p0s2rwkbdx5.note: Based on Richter 2011, 2016 with focus on Marine Isotope Stage 4-3.

p0s2rwktj4g.label: Mousterian of Acheulean Tradition
p0s2rwktj4g.note:
Mousterian of Acheulean Tradition is distinguished by handaxes, often triangular and cordiform.

Based on Soressi dissertation 2002.

p0s2rwk8kwp.label: Szeletian
p0s2rwk8kwp.note: Bifacial industries of the very late Middle Paleolithic, from about end of Marine Isotope Stage 5a or beginning of Marine Isotope Stage 4 to end of Middle Paleolithic.

p0s2rwkj466.label: Khormusan
p0s2rwkj466.note: Old name for technocomplex in Egypt and Sudan, Nubian, was Upper Paleolithic now Middle Paleolithic.

p0s2rwkrh4r.label: Micoquian
p0s2rwkrh4r.note:
Bifacial retouch frequent, Keilmesser.

Includes Keilmesser Group, partially based on Rchter 2011, Jöris 2004, using Marine Isotope Stage 5-3.

p0s2rwkq2c8.label: Aterian
p0s2rwkq2c8.note:
Tanged points, Levallois technology.

Especially in Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria, type site is Bir el Ater in Algeria, dates expanded according to Richter et al. 2010 with regard to Aterian at Ifri n Ammar.

p0s2rwk3x68.label: Charentian La Ferrassie
p0s2rwk3x68.note:
High Levallois component.

Follows general dating of Mousterian.

p0s2rwkw6zf.label: Charentian La Quina
p0s2rwkw6zf.note:
No or very few handaxes, many sidescrapers, often Quina type, very low, if any, Levallois component.

Follows general dating of Mousterian.

p0s2rwkwgnt.label: Mousterian
p0s2rwkwgnt.note: Based on Richter 2011, 2016 with focus on Marine Isotope Stage 8-3.

p0s2rwkwcmr.label: Late MSA
p0s2rwkwcmr.note:
Defined at Sibudu Cave for Late Middle Stone Age industries dated at 47.7 ka (Jacobs et al. 2008), also includes Border Cave.

Poorly defined industries from the late Middle Stone Age, possibly equivalent to Magosian-Tshangulan in Zimbabwe.

p0s2rwk9zmd.label: Late Levalloiso-Mousterian
p0s2rwk9zmd.note:
Sub-triangular points, unidirectional and convergent cores.

Tabun B-type, Kebara.

p0s2rwkzthp.label: Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkzthp.note: General term for Middle Paleolithic assemblages, whether they are Levallois or not.

p0s2rwkzjgb.label: Mousterian
p0s2rwkzjgb.note: General term for Middle Paleolithic assemblages with Levallois technology.

p0s2rwk8gqf.label: non-Levalloiso-Mousterian
p0s2rwk8gqf.note:
Non-specific non-Levallois technology.

General term for Middle Paleolithic assemblages with non-Levallois technology.

p0s2rwkmnsj.label: MSA 3
p0s2rwkmnsj.note: Defined at Sibudu Cave for MSA industries after HP dated at 58.5 ka (Jacobs et al. 2008), also includes Border Cave.
p0s2rwkmnsj.editorialNote: More specific term (narrower spatiotemporal coverage) than Post-Howiesonspoort (defined for Southern Africa more broadly).

p0s2rwk3frc.label: Howiesonspoort
p0s2rwk3frc.note:
The Howiesonspoort industry is a technocomplex to be found in the southern region of the African continent (as in South Africa, Namibia, Zambia), characterised by geometric forms of backed parts of blades, sometimes named microliths, crescents or lunates.

The minimum & maximum ages are estimates/average values. See Lombard et al. 2012 for ages.

p0s2rwkhs2p.label: Middle Pietersburg
p0s2rwkhs2p.note: Conversation between Michaela Ecker and Lyn Wadley in 2011 defined Middle Pieterburg as pre-Howiesonspoort, but used here more broadly to also include Howiesonspoort.

p0s2rwkhrsn.label: Pre-Howiesonspoort
p0s2rwkhrsn.note: Used especially at sites with no Still Bay.
p0s2rwkhrsn.editorialNote: More general term (broader spatiotemporal coverage) than MSA 3.

p0s2rwkpnk7.label: Bambata
p0s2rwkpnk7.note:
Equates to Rhodesian Still Bay in Zimbabwe.

Before 1965 Still Bay used for all sites with points, see also Pietersburg.

p0s2rwk5sfq.label: Still Bay
p0s2rwk5sfq.note:
The Still Bay lithic industry is characterized by bifacial points of lanceolate shape, the so-called Still Bay Points.

The minimum & maximum ages are estimates/average values. See Lombard et al. 2012 for ages.

p0s2rwk2374.label: Mossel Bay
p0s2rwk2374.note:
Triangular points with convergent flakes (Goodwin and van Riet Lowe 1929), Wurz uses term for pre-Still Bay of Klasies River.

The Mossel Bay lithic industry is characterized by bifacial points, sometimes used as a synonym for Still Bay. The minimum and maximum ages are estimated based on Lombard et al. 2012. See Keller 1970 (SAAB) for description.

Alternate labels based on Wurz S, 2002. Variability in the Middle Stone Age Lithic Sequence, 115,000–60,000 Years Ago at Klasies River, South Africa. Journal of Archaeological Science 29, 1001–1015.

p0s2rwk3smr.label: Pre-Still Bay
p0s2rwk3smr.note: Ante-Still Bay, the time before Still Bay generally speaking, broader than pre-Still Bay proposed by Lombard et al. 2012.

p0s2rwkd5xr.label: Early MSA
p0s2rwkd5xr.note: Early Middle Stone Age includes those assemblages that are older than Still Bay.

p0s2rwkv6vb.label: Glen Grey Falls
p0s2rwkv6vb.note: Seldom used and poorly defined industry in sequence starting with Glen Grey Falls, Pietersburg, Still Bay, Howiesonspoort, proposed by Goodwin and van Riet Lowe 1929, dates are highly speculative.

p0s2rwkqfc4.label: Middle Levalloiso-Mousterian
p0s2rwkqfc4.note:
Shorter blades and oval to rectangular flakes, centripetal and bidirectional cores.

Tabun C-type.

p0s2rwkrdwh.label: Klasies River
p0s2rwkrdwh.note:
Alternate labels based on Wurz S, 2002. Variability in the Middle Stone Age Lithic Sequence, 115,000–60,000 Years Ago at Klasies River, South Africa. Journal of Archaeological Science 29, 1001–1015.

See Lombard et al. 2012 for estimated dates.

p0s2rwk3mdp.label: Late Acheulean
p0s2rwk3mdp.note:
Conceived for Indian sites with refined bifaces and prepared core technologies. Blumenschine et al. (1983) first classified such assemblages as Middle Paleolithic, but more recently they have been grouped as Lower Paleolithic.

Age range consistent with relatively young sites in Middle Son Valley in India.

p0s2rwkkxgq.label: Acheulean
p0s2rwkkxgq.note:
Conceived for Indian sites with a general Acheulean affiliation, especially including sites with bifacial technology.

Wide age range consistent with oldest (Attirampakkam) and youngest (Middle Son Valley) sites in India.

p0s2rwktwhb.label: MSA 1
p0s2rwktwhb.note: Volman Middle Stone Age 1, early Middle Stone Age, see Lombard et al. 2012 for estimated age.

p0s2rwkb97f.label: Early Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkb97f.note:
Includes those assemblages that are of non-specific Early Middle Paleolithic attribution.

Misliya Cave.

p0s2rwkq335.label: Late Sangoan
p0s2rwkq335.note: Early Stone Age to Middle Stone Age Transition, see Charaman, for now set to same age as Sangoan.

p0s2rwk6cpw.label: Lupemban
p0s2rwk6cpw.note:
Latest phase of Early Stone Age - Ojallo Industry / Earliest phase of Middle Stone Age  - Pundo Makwar Industry.

Early Stone Age to Middle Stone Age Transition.

p0s2rwkh4jw.label: Proto-Still Bay
p0s2rwkh4jw.note:
More heavy duty picks and core-axes, small scrapers, rare handaxes and cleavers.

Early Stone Age to Middle Stone Age  Transition, similar to Sangoan.

p0s2rwkznpv.label: Sangoan
p0s2rwkznpv.note:
Poss proto-Still Bay, 1st Intermediate (Klein): Charama, Bembesi in Zimbabwe/ Sango Bay, Twin Rivers, Khami, Pomongwe, Nsongezi, Kalambo Falls in Zambia/ Bambata?

Early Stone Age to Middle Stone Age  Transition.

p0s2rwkwcdz.label: Early Pietersburg
p0s2rwkwcdz.note: Conversation between Michaela Ecker and Lyn Wadley in 2011 defines Early Pietersburg as pre-Still Bay, but consider Proto-Still Bay for comparison.

p0s2rwkvtbj.label: Early Levalloiso-Mousterian
p0s2rwkvtbj.note:
Blades, elongated forms, unidirectional and bidirectional cores.

Tabun D-type.

p0s2rwkt9hw.label: Early Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkt9hw.note: Broad interpretation, but applied to sites in France and Italy.

p0s2rwk9s3n.label: ESA/MSA

en: Early Stone Age to Middle Stone Age Transition

p0s2rwk9s3n.note:
Transitional phase between Early Stone Age (ESA) and Middle Stone Age (MSA).

Following van Riet Lowe, Clark, Klein, Mitchell, Barham, and others, for vague and diverse industries.

p0s2rwkzgmz.label: Acheulo-Yabrudian
p0s2rwkzgmz.note:
Synonymous with Amudian, Mugharan Tradition, Pre-Aurignacian.

Lower to Middle Paleolithic Transition, includes Tabun E, Qesem.

p0s2rwk5gvx.label: Amudian
p0s2rwk5gvx.note:
Synonymous with Pre-Aurignacian, Mugharan Tradition, Acheulo-Yabrudian.

Lower to Middle Paleolithic Transition, esimate based on dates for Qesem, Yabroud, Zuttiyeh, Tabun.

p0s2rwk5xwm.label: Mugharan Tradition
p0s2rwk5xwm.note:
Synonymous with Amudian, Acheulo-Yabrudian, Pre-Aurignacian.

Lower to Middle Paleolithic Transition.

p0s2rwkr2b6.label: Pre-Aurignacian
p0s2rwkr2b6.note:
Synonymous with Amudian, Mugharan Tradition, Acheulo-Yabrudian, includes Levallois and prismatic blade cores.

Lower to Middle Paleolithic Transition, defined by Rust for Yabrud, Syria, dates estimated.

p0s2rwkdv6q.label: Tayacian
p0s2rwkdv6q.note:
Equivalent to Tabun F-type in Israel.

Obsolete techno-complex, use Late Acheulean - Levant, age range probably narrower. Sometimes used to describe Low and Mid Paleolithic flake industries lacking handaxes, bifaces and retouched pieces. Originally used for industries from lower levels at La Micoque, subsequently applied to industries over wide geographical and chronol range. Layers belonging to penultimate glacial period assigned to Tayacian. Also describes primitive flake-tool tradition of Israel, like smaller Clactonian industry.

p0s2rwk379x.label: Acheulean
p0s2rwk379x.note:
General Acheulean techno-complexes from Europe.

Earliest possible dates of 700000 in the Loire valley of France, dates from ca. 800000 to 1000000 in Barranc de la Boella, Spain.

p0s2rwkpsb6.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkpsb6.note: General Lower Paleolithic with no further details.

p0s2rwk4vvk.label: LP/MP Transitional Industries
p0s2rwk4vvk.note:
Latest phase of Lower Paleolithic or earliest phase of Middle Paleolithic in Europe, defined through Italy at Guado San Nicola.

Lower Paleolithic to Middle Paleolithic Transition.

p0s2rwkjp52.label: Clactonian
p0s2rwkjp52.note:
Clactonian techno-complexes from Europe.

Earliest possible dates not known, date estimated on Jöris 2014, Oxygen Isotope Stage 16-9.

p0s2rwkf28k.label: Fauresmith
p0s2rwkf28k.note:
Last phase of the Acheulean.

See 1st Intermediate phase of Richard G. Klein.

p0s2rwkjtbj.label: Late Acheulean
p0s2rwkjtbj.note:
Last phase of the Acheulean with well developed and elaborated handaxes.

Sites include Transvaal, Montagu, Rooidam. we chose 300 ka for consistency with Acheulean, but according to Deacon & Deacon (1999) up to 250 ka and Mitchell (2002) up to 200 ka.

p0s2rwk5sjm.label: Victoria West
p0s2rwk5sjm.note:
Proto-Levallois cores, horseshoe-shaped cores, prepared cores (e.g. Montagu Cave).

See Victoria West I & II, proto-Levallois cores (Goodwin), Stellenbosch, Chellean, described in Barham & Mitchell 2008 as Middle Pleistocene ESA, but with undefined appearance.

p0s2rwkp552.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkp552.note: General Lower Paleolithic with no further details.

p0s2rwk8scs.label: Acheulean
p0s2rwk8scs.note:
Handaxe cultures of the Acheulean.

See also Abbevillian.

p0s2rwknm9c.label: ESA
p0s2rwknm9c.note: Includes assemblages that cannot be attributed to a specific phase of the Early Stone Age.

p0s2rwkc67v.label: Early Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkc67v.note: Added for oldest early Middle Paleolithic site in India, Attirampakkam, with prepared core technology and diminutive bifaces (based on date range 321-449 ka).

p0s2rwkx727.label: Acheulean
p0s2rwkx727.note: Use this term for Levantine Acheulean assemblages.

p0s2rwk2zd3.label: Middle Acheulean
p0s2rwk2zd3.note: Ubeidiya, Latamne, Umm Khatafa, early Middle Pleistocene assemblages.

p0s2rwk998h.label: Middle Acheulean
p0s2rwk998h.note:
Middle phase of Acheulean.

See Victoria West I & II, proto-Levallois cores (Goodwin), Stellenbosch, Chellean.

p0s2rwkftrf.label: Developed Oldowan
p0s2rwkftrf.note:
A) 1.65-1.53 Ma, spheroids, small flake tools, B) 1.53-1.2 Ma, and small percentage of bifacially flaked tools, shaping of anvils, more LCTs, C) 1.2-1.0 Ma, more percussion tools, variable bifaces.

Mitchell & Barham (2008) say Oldowan and Acheulean overlap in time.

p0s2rwkzcfq.label: Early Acheulean
p0s2rwkzcfq.note:
Oldest phase of the Acheulean.

Kokiselei 4, Sterkfontein, Swartkrans.

p0s2rwkqm5m.label: Oldowan
p0s2rwkqm5m.note:
Use this term for  Oldowan assemblages in the Levant.

Dmanisi, Erq el-Ahmar.

p0s2rwk8vhh.label: Karari Industry
p0s2rwk8vhh.note:
Similar to Developed Oldowan, with a conspicuous incidence of core scrapers.

The formal category Karari Industry has been proposed to designate assemblages from the Lower Okote Member. This industry displays a rather loose, heterogeneous set of characteristics. Assemblages exemplifying these characteristics are to be understood as a facies of variable sets of toolkits. This industry shares broad, generalized features with near-contemporary industries such as the Developed Oldowan A from Bed II at Olduvai, but also show distinctive patterns of difference.

p0s2rwkrsmz.label: KBS Industry
p0s2rwkrsmz.note:
Like Oldowan but with rarity of retouched flakes (small scrapers).

Industry deriving from the Kay Behrensmeyer Site (KBS) tuff and KBS member of Koobi Fora. The assemblages are comparable to Olduvai Bed I. The only difference – and therefore the distinction – is the rarity of retouched flakes (small scrapers). But since these assemblages are broadly contemporary, the KBS Industry should be seen as a local variant of the Oldowan industry.

p0s2rwkgzwv.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkgzwv.note: General LP techno-complexes from S Asia, with ages parallel to the Acheulean. However, there is no clear distinction between those two technocomplexes. Thus far, there is no evidence for pre-Acheulean cultures in South Asia.
p0s2rwkgzwv.editorialNote: Date range adjusted as of June 2024.

p0s2rwkvgft.label: Early Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwkvgft.note: General EUP techno-complexes from E Asia.

p0s2rwk59gd.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwk59gd.note: General LP techno-complexes from E Asia.

p0s2rwkv9kq.label: Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwkv9kq.note: General UP techno-complexes from E Asia.

p0s2rwkjpgp.label: Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkjpgp.note:
In general, MP finds are made of poor quality local raw material, using direct-hard hammer percussion without preparing cores. Regular flakes often used as they are, but some shaped regular tools, mainly side scrapers are present. Technology is often simple free-hand core reduction or bipolar technique. Some diversity does exist, as shown by the Huangniliang site in NE China.

The Middle Paleolithic in China is also referred to as later Early Paleolithic and Late Paleolithic.

p0s2rwkt85p.label: Early Pleistocene
p0s2rwkt85p.note:
General Early Pleistocene techno-complexes from E Asia without diagnostic artifacts but dated to Early Pleistocene.

We need to reconsider this in the future.

p0s2rwkqdqs.label: Late Acheulean
p0s2rwkqdqs.note:
Conceived for Chinese sites with questionable bifaces, as well as picks, cleavers, choppers and spheroids. Example is from Yang et al. 2014 who discusses chopper-chopping tool industry.

Age range is based on mammalian biostratigraphy, so not strictly reliable.

p0s2rwkjqsm.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkjqsm.note: Includes pebble cultures from Asia, but not South and East Asia, or the Levant.

p0s2rwkf3rz.label: Middle Pleistocene
p0s2rwkf3rz.note:
General Middle Pleistocene techno-complexes from E Asia without diagnostic artifacts but dated to Middle Pleistocene.

We need to reconsider this in the future.

p0s2rwkj4cn.label: Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwkj4cn.note:
Sites with undefined Upper Paleolithic technologies, usually includes laminar debitage but not microliths.

Age range based on max age for microlithic industries and general min age for Pleistocene.

p0s2rwkpv3m.label: Late Pleistocene
p0s2rwkpv3m.note:
General Late Pleistocene techno-complexes from E Asia without diagnostic artifacts but dated to Late Pleistocene.

We need to reconsider this in the future.

p0s2rwkvtvz.label: Holocene
p0s2rwkvtvz.note: General term for undefined, probably Holocene assemblages.

p0s2rwk37b8.label: Late Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwk37b8.note: General category for Late Middle Paleolithic assemblages from Eurasia, but not the Levant.

p0s2rwkp9zv.label: Late Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkp9zv.note: Vaguely defined entity based on Bhimbetka caves. At Patne, the authors assign artefacts to advanced MP, which we equate with late MP. They describe a flake based industry with some UP attributes. We base the minimum age on the dates for the MP and the maximum age of the latest Acheulean industries of India. This means that the MP and LP overlap significantly.

p0s2rwk98c5.label: Late Pleistocene
p0s2rwk98c5.note: General Late Pleistocene techno-complexes from SE Asia without diagnostic artifacts but dated to Late Pleistocene, including possible Middle and Upper Paleolithic cultures. Project may need to reconsider this in the future.

p0s2rwkrjbs.note: "Generic Paleolithic" period definition not used to describe ROCEEH-ROAD data, but added to authority in order to align ROCEEH dataset properly with ARIADNE.

p046hphpgdz.label: Burica Phase
p046hphpgdz.note: “No radiocarbon dates are available as yet to establish the beginnings of the Burica Phase. I have nevertheless placed them at A.D. 300-500. This estimate is based on the presence of Coclé sherds, probably Early Coclé, and a possible Venado Beach sherd in levels of this phase… The terminal date of A.D. 800 for our Burica Phase is tentatively based on the radiocarbon date for the next phase.” (p. 86)

p046hphwgfm.label: San Lorenzo Phase
p046hphwgfm.note: “The next occupation in the Chiriquí Gulf is the San Lorenzo Phase which I have tentatively placed between A.D. 800 and A.D. 1100… An estimate for the end of this phase is around A.D. 1100, based on estimates for the beginning of the next phase.” (p. 86)

p046hphr2qz.label: Chiriquí Phase
p046hphr2qz.note: “The beginnings of our Chiriquí Phase should be placed in the Gulf at around A.D. 1100… A terminal date for the Chiriquí Phase should be placed at the time of the Conquest (A.D. 1500) or slightly later.” (p. 86)

source.title: Cultural chronology of the Gulf of Chiriquí, Panama

p046hph.editorialNote: The entire work discusses evidence for both relative and absolute chronologies in the are of the Gulf of Chiriquí, but the periods discussed are only given clear absolute dates on page 86.

p04k9nh58qr.label: Aguas Buenas
p04k9nh58qr.note:
“For decades, the A.D. 600  eruption of Volcán Barú was assumed to have been catastrophic enough to have ended Aguas Buenas settlements across much of the region (Linares 1977:313, 1980e:245; Sheets 2004)”, but “it appears that both the A.D. 600 eruption and assumptions about the lack of early populations in the Caribbean watershed need to be rethought. Like the rest of Gran Chiriquí, the Aguas Buenas in Gran Chiriquí might have lasted until A.D. 800 or later (Corrales 2000).” (pp 74-75) 

“In Western Panama, the Aguas Buenas has three different names. The most used is the Bugaba (with early and late halves), coined by Spang et al. (1980) to refer to ceramics in highland Chiriquí and the Caribbean coast (Kudarauskas et al. 1980). The second is the Burica (A.D. 400-600), used by Linares (1968) to describe Aguas Buenas materials on the Pacific coast. The least used is the Barriles phase (400  B.C. to A.D. 200), described by Haberland  (1976).” (p. 75)
p04k9nh58qr.editorialNote: While Palumbo presents “Aguas Buenas” as the primary label in the text, he focuses elsewhere on the term “Bugaba”. He also underlines the heterogeneity of interpretation concerning this period in scholarship on the area; differences emerge in the consideration of the period as a stylistic, demographic/ethic, or political phenomenon.

p04k9nhsk6n.label: San Lorenzo Phase
p04k9nhsk6n.note: “San Lorenzo ceramics have been described as a temporal phase by Linares (1968a, 1968b)” (p. 76).

p04k9nh2c7q.label: Concepción Phase
p04k9nh2c7q.note: "... pottery appears relatively late in the Chiriquí sequence with the introduction of Concepción wares around 300 B.C. The Concepción represents the adoption or introduction of ceramic technology in Western Panama." (p. 68)

p04k9nhtbcj.label: Chiriquí Phase
p04k9nhtbcj.spatialCoverageDescription: Western Panama; parts of Costa Rica
p04k9nhtbcj.note: “The Chiriquí phase (also called the Boruca, Palmer, or Sierpe in parts of Costa Rica) is the best known of all the Gran Chiriquí time periods.” (p. 77)

source.title: The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama
source.citation: Palumbo, S. 2009. The Development of Complex Society in the Volcán Barú Region of Western Panama. Unpublished PhD thesis, University of Pittsburgh.

p04k9nh.editorialNote: Although the information in this dissertation has not been published separately, Palumbo is a cited authority in the field, and the period information in the dissertation is supported by extensive citation of public work. One period, "Tropical Forest Archaic", has been omitted here because it is not clear if its dates are expressed correctly (the period is assigned to 4800-2300 BCE, but in other sources its second phase ends in 300 BCE).

p0j5449rp49.label: Talamanca Phase
p0j5449rp49.editorialNote: This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43.

p0j5449ghdk.label: Boquete Phase
p0j5449ghdk.editorialNote: This definition is provided in a contribution by Ranere to the edited volume: A. Ranere, “Preceramic shelters in the Talamancan Range”, pp. 16-43.

p0j5449tz3h.label: Tropical Forest Archaic
p0j5449tz3h.editorialNote: This definition is provided in Linares' concluding chapter, but makes reference to the preceding chapters, including Ranere's: O. Linares, "Conclusions", pp. 233-247.

source.title: Adaptive radiations in prehistoric Panama
source.citation: Adaptive Radiations in Prehistoric Panama, eds. Olga Linares and Anthony Ranere, Peabody Museum Monographs Number 5, Harvard University: Cambridge, MA, 1980.

p0j5449.editorialNote: Although the periods in this authority are derived from two separate contributions to this work by Linares and Ranere, they are closely connected enough to represent claims that could be considered to be made by the work as a whole.

p06tnbvxq74.label: Talamanca phase
p06tnbvxq74.note: The older of the two preceramic phases, Talamanca, has been dated by Ranere (1975b: 177) to before 3000 B.C., while Cooke (1976a:22) suggested a dating between 5000 and 3000 B.C. Taking the corrected C14 dates into account, 6000 to 3000 B.C. seems appropriate.” (p. 236)

p06tnbvtdjr.label: Boquete phase
p06tnbvtdjr.note: The Boquete lithic assemblage “stratigraphically overlies the Talamanca phase at the Casita de Piedra and Trapiche rockshelters (Ranere 1975b: 176-77). The single C14 date, slightly later than 3000 B.C. when adjusted, came from the top of layer D at Casita de Piedra and either antedates the Boquete phase or reflects its very beginning (Linares and Ranere 1971: 350). The end should be around 1000 B.C., since SI-1844 is said to date the transition to the following ceramic phase at Casita de Piedra. Boquete represents a gradual development out of the Talamanca phase.” (p. 237)

source.title: The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui
source.citation: Wolfgang Haberland, 1984. “The Archaeology of Greater Chiriqui”. In Frederick Lange and Doris Stone, eds., The Archaeology of Lower Central America. Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press, pp. 233-262.

p0jqmd78gc8.label: Roman Climate Optimum
p0jqmd78gc8.note: "The empire reached its maximal extent and prosperity in the folds of a late Holocene climate period called the Roman Climate Optimum (RCO)." (p.14)

p0jqmd7ftd8.label: Roman Transitional Period
p0jqmd7ftd8.note: "... a period of climate disorganization covering three centuries (AD 150-450) set in, which we will propose to call the Roman Transitional Period." (p.15)

p0jqmd7fkfq.label: Late Antique Little Ice Age
p0jqmd7fkfq.note: "... from the later fifth century, we sense the stirrings of a decisive reorganization that culminated in the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A spasm of volcanic activity in the AD 530s and 540s brought on the most frigid spell in the entire Late Holocene." (p. 15)

source.title: The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire
source.citation: Harper, K. 2017. The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton N. J.: Princeton University Press.

p0f66wqth44.label: Pre-Christian Iceland
p0f66wqth44.note: Iceland was Christianized in the year 1000 CE, when Christianity became the religion by law. In Icelandic, this event is known as the kristnitaka (literally, "the taking of Christianity"). (from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianization_of_Iceland).
p0f66wqth44.editorialNote: The start date of 870 is a widely accepted but rough approximation of the settlement of Iceland.

p0f66wqfrs4.label: Settlement Period, Iceland
p0f66wqfrs4.note: Traditionally, the Icelandic Age of Settlement is considered to have lasted from 874 to 930, at which point most of the island had been claimed and Alþingi (Althingi), the assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth, was founded at Þingvellir (Thingvellir). (from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_Iceland).
p0f66wqfrs4.editorialNote: The start date of 870 is a widely accepted but rough approximation of the settlement of Iceland.

source.title: The settlement of Iceland : a story from the ninth and tenth centuries

p0s84tqvjs7.label: Late antiquity (Roman Noricum)
p0s84tqvjs7.editorialNote: While Gassner et al. (pages 371–372) define Late Antiquity in their book form AD 284 until AD 610, at this place AD 488, when Odoaker ordered parts of the remaining Roman people moving from Noricum to Italy (page 372), is used as a stop of the period. AD 488 is the commonly used date for marking the definite end of *Roman* Noricum and the beginning of the Early Medieval Period in that area (although the Western Roman Empire ceased to be in AD 476); nevertheless, various settlements continued in the Early Medieval Period, as well as seemingly not all Romans moved to Italy and stayed instead in Noricum.

p0s84tq9w22.label: Roman antiquity (Roman Noricum)
p0s84tq9w22.editorialNote: The period subsumes from the overarching periods defined for Roman Noricum ("Early Period," "Imperial Period," and "Late Antiquity"; derived from Hagmann 2021, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0s84tq>). Furthermore, this overarching period takes into account the early pre-occupation activities in the area of the urban settlement at the Magdalensberg ("Stadt auf dem Magdalensberg", Carinthia/AUT), the beginning of which is put around 50 BC (cf., Gassner et al. 2002–2003, 70. 369). Finally, in addition to the absolute early period, the highly late period between 488 and 500 AD is also considered, in the context of which, according to "classical" doctrine and in view of the written tradition (vita Sancti Severini), 488 AD a settlement of the remaining Roman population (so-called "Romanen" in German-speaking research) should have already taken place and which represents a historically highly ambiguous period during the transition to the early Middle Ages (cf., Eichert - Richards 2022, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0cwwzn>).

p0s84tq35sg.label: Early period (northern Roman Noricum)
p0s84tq35sg.editorialNote: While the early Roman period for southern Noricum started earlier (cf. Hagmann 2021, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0ndpcqbmxk>), due to the historical development, a significant establishment of a Roman settlement in the Danubian area (which corresponds to northern Noricum) can only be expected around or after AD 50 (cf., Hagmann, Dominik, 2022. A "Roman Rural Landscape" in Northeastern Noricum: Results of Landscape Archaeological Investigations on Rural Settlement of the Roman Imperial Period in Lower Austria. In Franz Pieler/Wolfgang Breibert (eds.), Contributions to the Lower Austrian Regional Archaeology Day 2022, pp. 61-70. Scientific Publications from the Regional Collections of Lower Austria Asparn/Zaya, <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6751583>).

p0s84tq2ndm.label: Roman antiquity (northern Roman Noricum)
p0s84tq2ndm.editorialNote: The period describes the whole timespan of Roman interactions, specifically for northern Roman Noricum, which corresponds to the Danube region. The period contains the overarching periods defined for northern Roman Noricum ("Early Period (northern Roman Noricum)," "Imperial Period," and "Late Antiquity"; derived from Hagmann 2021, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0s84tq>). While the early Roman period for southern Noricum started earlier (cf. Hagmann 2021, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0ndpcqbmxk>), due to the historical development, a significant establishment of a Roman settlement in the Danubian area (which corresponds to northern Noricum) can only be expected around or after AD 50 (cf., Hagmann, Dominik, 2022. A "Roman Rural Landscape" in Northeastern Noricum: Results of Landscape Archaeological Investigations on Rural Settlement of the Roman Imperial Period in Lower Austria. In Franz Pieler/Wolfgang Breibert (eds.), Contributions to the Lower Austrian Regional Archaeology Day 2022, pp. 61-70. Scientific Publications from the Regional Collections of Lower Austria Asparn/Zaya, <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6751583>). Furthermore, in addition to the absolute early period, the highly late period between 488 and 500 AD is also considered, in the context of which, according to "classical" doctrine and in view of the written tradition (vita Sancti Severini), 488 AD a settlement of the remaining Roman population (so-called "Romanen" in German-speaking research) should have already taken place and which represents a historically highly ambiguous period during the transition to the early Middle Ages (cf., Eichert - Richards 2022, <http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0cwwzn>).
